Can I change plans anytime? Yes. Upgrades take effect immediately with a prorated charge. Downgrades within the same monthly cadence also take effect immediately, with credit applied to your next bill. Downgrades on annual plans (and any switch between monthly and annual) are scheduled to take effect at the end of the period you've already paid for — no refund or extra charge today, and you keep your current plan limits until the switch happens. You can cancel a scheduled change at any time before it takes effect. What happens when I hit my monitor limit? You won't lose any existing monitors. You simply won't be able to create new ones until you upgrade or remove existing monitors. All active monitors continue running normally. Do you offer annual billing? Yes. Use the Monthly / Annual toggle above the pricing tiers. Annual plans are priced at 10× the monthly rate, so you get two months free compared to paying monthly. The plan limits and features are identical — only the billing cadence changes. You can switch between monthly and annual at any time; switches take effect at the end of your current paid period. What payment methods do you accept? We accept all major credit and debit cards (Visa, Mastercard, American Express), PayPal, Google Pay, and Apple Pay through Paddle. Enterprise plans can pay via invoice. Can I cancel anytime? Absolutely. No contracts, no cancellation fees. If you cancel, your plan remains active until the end of the current billing period, then reverts to the Free tier. What's the difference between monitors and heartbeat monitors? Regular monitors actively check your endpoints at set intervals (HTTP, DNS, TCP, ICMP). Heartbeat monitors work the other way — your service sends a ping to DevHelm, and you get alerted if the ping stops arriving. Useful for cron jobs, background workers, and scheduled tasks. Is there a free trial of paid plans? The Free tier is your trial — 50 monitors with full CLI/SDK/Terraform access and dependency tracking. There's no time limit. DevHelm is a monitoring and incident management platform built for engineering teams. Define your monitors, alert channels, and incident policies in code — deploy them with a single command or a Git push.  Uptime Monitoring HTTP, TCP, DNS, ICMP, MCP server, and heartbeat monitors with configurable check intervals, probe regions, and assertion rules. Incident Management Automated incident creation from monitor failures, severity escalation, confirmation policies, and recovery tracking. Alerting Route alerts to Slack, PagerDuty, OpsGenie, Discord, Microsoft Teams, email, webhooks, and 13 more integrations with escalation chains and notification policies. Monitoring as Code Define your entire monitoring stack in YAML or Terraform. Version it, review it, deploy it from CI. Webhook Testing Capture the webhooks your system sends in an inbox, then wait for and assert on them from tests. Email Testing Receive mail on a testing domain and read OTP codes and links from tests and CI.  ​ How it works  1 Define your monitors Write a devhelm.yml file or use the CLI, SDK, or Dashboard to configure HTTP, TCP, DNS, ICMP, MCP server, or heartbeat monitors with check intervals, regions, and assertions. 2 Connect alert channels Route failures to Slack, PagerDuty, OpsGenie, Discord, Teams, email, webhooks, or any of the 20 supported integrations. Build escalation chains with acknowledgment and repeat rules. 3 Deploy Run devhelm deploy or push to Git. The DevHelm GitHub Action validates and applies your configuration automatically. 4 Respond to incidents When a monitor fails, DevHelm opens an incident, alerts your team through your notification policies, and tracks the timeline. Incidents auto-resolve when the monitor recovers.  ​ Developer surfaces  DevHelm meets you where you work:  Surface Install Description CLI npm i -g devhelm Full monitor management, YAML deploy, imperative and declarative workflows TypeScript SDK npm i @devhelm/sdk Typed client for Node.js and browser Python SDK pip install devhelm Typed client for Python 3.11+ Terraform Provider Registry Manage monitors as Terraform resources MCP Server uvx devhelm-mcp-server (PyPI) AI-native interface for Cursor, Claude Desktop GitHub Action Marketplace CI/CD integration for config-as-code deploys REST API — Full HTTP API with OpenAPI spec  ​ Next steps  Quickstart Create your first monitor in under 5 minutes. An SLA calculator converts a service level agreement percentage (like 99.9%) into the exact amount of downtime that percentage allows per day, week, month, and year. Use it when negotiating SLAs with vendors, setting internal availability targets, or checking whether a provider stayed within their commitment after an outage. How is allowed downtime calculated? The formula is: Allowed downtime = Period × (1 − SLA / 100). For a 99.9% SLA over a 30.44-day month, that's 2,629,746 seconds × 0.001 = 2,630 seconds, or about 43 minutes 50 seconds. This calculator uses 365.2425 days/year and 30.4369 days/month for precision. How much downtime is 99.9% uptime? 99.9% uptime (three nines) allows 1 minute 26 seconds of downtime per day, 10 minutes 5 seconds per week, 43 minutes 50 seconds per month, and 8 hours 46 minutes per year. Most SaaS products target this level as the baseline for production services. What is the difference between 99.9% and 99.99% uptime? 99.9% allows about 8 hours 46 minutes of downtime per year, while 99.99% (four nines) allows only 52 minutes 34 seconds. Each additional nine requires exponentially more investment in redundancy, failover automation, and operational discipline. Most web apps target 99.9%; critical financial infrastructure targets 99.99% or higher. How do I calculate uptime percentage from observed downtime? Uptime % = ((Total period − Downtime) / Total period) × 100. For example, 2 hours of downtime in a 30-day month: ((720 − 2) / 720) × 100 = 99.722%. Use the "Downtime → Uptime %" mode above to calculate this instantly. What SLA target should I choose? It depends on the cost of downtime to your users. 99% is reasonable for internal tools, 99.9% for most SaaS products, 99.95%+ for services where outages directly cost customers money. Don't chase five nines as a vanity metric — the infrastructure cost grows exponentially while the user-perceptible difference shrinks. An error budget is the maximum amount of unreliability your SLO allows within a given time window. If your SLO is 99.9%, your error budget is 0.1% of total requests (or time). Once the budget is exhausted, the team should prioritize reliability over new features. How does burn rate work? Burn rate measures how fast you're consuming your error budget. A burn rate of 1x means you'll exhaust the budget exactly at the end of the window. 2x means you'll run out halfway through. Google SRE recommends alerting at 14.4x (2% budget in 1 hour) and 6x (5% budget in 6 hours). What happens when the error budget is exhausted? The typical policy is to freeze feature releases and redirect engineering effort to reliability work — fixing bugs, adding redundancy, improving alerting — until the budget recovers in the next window or a new budget period begins. What's the difference between SLO, SLA, and SLI? SLI (Service Level Indicator) is a measurement — e.g. proportion of successful requests. SLO (Service Level Objective) is the internal target — e.g. 99.9% of requests succeed. SLA (Service Level Agreement) is the contractual promise to customers, usually with financial penalties. A cron expression is a string of five (or six) fields separated by spaces that defines a schedule. The standard five fields are: minute (0–59), hour (0–23), day of month (1–31), month (1–12), and day of week (0–6, Sunday=0). Special characters like * (any), */n (every n), and ranges (1-5) add flexibility. What does */5 mean in a cron expression? The */5 syntax means 'every 5th unit.' In the minute field, */5 means every 5 minutes (0, 5, 10, 15, …). In the hour field, */5 means every 5 hours (0, 5, 10, 15, 20). What's the difference between cron and crontab? Cron is the daemon (background service) that executes scheduled commands. Crontab is the file or command used to create, edit, and list the schedule entries. 'crontab -e' opens your personal schedule for editing. Can I use cron for monitoring schedules? Yes — monitoring tools like DevHelm use cron-like intervals to schedule health checks. For example, '*/5 * * * *' would check every 5 minutes. DevHelm supports intervals from 30 seconds up to configurable cron schedules for synthetic monitoring. Navigation Terraform Provider Terraform Provider Docs Guides Integrations API Reference CLI Monitoring as Code SDKs Learn Overview Overview YAML Format File Format Monitors Alert Channels Notification Policies Tags & Secrets Deploy Workflow Workflow Drift & Locking Terraform Provider Quickstart Overview Monitors Alert Channels Tags Data Sources Importing CI/CD CI/CD Patterns Overview GitHub Actions Generic CI Multi-Environment On this page Install Available resources Available data sources Quick example Import existing resources When to use Terraform vs YAML Next steps Terraform Provider Terraform Provider Copy page Copy page Manage DevHelm monitors, alert channels, status pages, and more as Terraform resources Copy page Copy page The DevHelm Terraform provider lets you manage your monitoring stack — monitors, alert channels, status pages, secrets, and more — declaratively alongside your cloud infrastructure.  The provider is published on the Terraform Registry as devhelmhq/devhelm .  Status: Beta. The schema is stable, the resource set is feature-complete against the DevHelm v1 API, and the provider has been validated end-to-end against production. While the other DevHelm surfaces (CLI, SDKs, MCP server) are now at 1.0.0 , the Terraform provider is intentionally held at 0.2.0-beta.x for a short soak window to harden a defense-in-depth rollback path. Safe for production use; pin the exact version below.  ​ Install  terraform {  required_version = ">= 1.5.0"  required_providers {  devhelm = {  source = "devhelmhq/devhelm"  version = "0.2.0-beta.7"  }  }  }   provider "devhelm" {}   Pre-release pin required. The provider currently ships only as pre-release versions, and Terraform’s ~> operator never selects pre-releases. Pin the exact version above ( 0.2.0-beta.7 is the latest published tag); bump it explicitly when the next version ships, or wait for the GA 1.0.0 cut to switch to a range like ~> 1.0 . Latest version is on the Registry overview page .  All four provider attributes have environment-variable equivalents and are optional. The most common pattern is to leave the provider block empty and supply credentials through the environment so the same config works locally, in CI, and in Terraform Cloud.  Attribute Env var Default Description token DEVHELM_API_TOKEN — Required. Create under Settings → API Keys in the Dashboard . Sensitive. base_url DEVHELM_API_URL https://api.devhelm.io API endpoint org_id DEVHELM_ORG_ID 1 Organization ID (multi-org tokens only) workspace_id DEVHELM_WORKSPACE_ID 1 Workspace ID (multi-workspace tokens only)  ​ Available resources  Resource Purpose devhelm_monitor HTTP, DNS, TCP, ICMP, Heartbeat, MCP Server monitors devhelm_alert_channel 20 channel types: Slack, Email, PagerDuty, OpsGenie, Discord, Teams, Webhook, Telegram, Google Chat, Pushover, Mattermost, Splunk On-Call, Pushbullet, Linear, Incident.io, Rootly, Zapier, Datadog, Jira, GitLab devhelm_notification_policy Routing rules from monitors → channels devhelm_webhook Outbound webhook subscriptions for platform events devhelm_secret Vault secrets referenced by monitor auth and config devhelm_environment Per-environment variable scopes (production, staging, …) devhelm_tag Tags for filtering and grouping devhelm_resource_group Service / team groupings devhelm_resource_group_membership Add a user to a resource group devhelm_dependency Track third-party SaaS components (GitHub, Stripe, …) devhelm_status_page Public or private status pages devhelm_status_page_component Components shown on a status page devhelm_status_page_component_group Group components into sections devhelm_status_page_custom_domain Custom domain attached to a status page devhelm_status_page_custom_domain_verification DNS / TLS verification record  ​ Available data sources  devhelm_monitor , devhelm_alert_channel , devhelm_environment , devhelm_resource_group , devhelm_service , devhelm_status_page , devhelm_tag . See Data sources .  ​ Quick example  resource "devhelm_tag" "production" {  name = "production"  color = "#10b981"  }   resource "devhelm_alert_channel" "ops_slack" {  name = "Engineering Slack"  channel_type = "slack"  webhook_url = var . slack_webhook_url  mention_text = "@channel"  }   resource "devhelm_monitor" "api_health" {  name = "API Health"  type = "HTTP"  frequency_seconds = 60  regions = [ "us-east" , "eu-west" ]   config = jsonencode ({  url = "https://api.example.com/health"  method = "GET"  verifyTls = true  })   assertions {  type = "status_code"  # `expected` is a STRING — quote even plain numeric codes. `200`  # (number) plans cleanly but apply fails with "Provider produced  # inconsistent result" because the API normalizes to "200" (string).  config = jsonencode ({ expected = "200" , operator = "equals" })  }   assertions {  type = "response_time"  config = jsonencode ({ thresholdMs = 2000 })  severity = "warn"  }   tag_ids = [ devhelm_tag . production . id ]  alert_channel_ids = [ devhelm_alert_channel . ops_slack . id ]  }   config and assertions[].config are JSON strings (not HCL blocks). Use jsonencode({...}) and camelCase field names — they map directly to the API wire format ( thresholdMs , verifyTls , expectedInterval , …). The provider validates the payload against the generated schema at plan time, so unknown fields fail fast.  ​ Import existing resources  Every resource supports terraform import except devhelm_status_page_custom_domain_verification (a synthetic verification barrier with no server-side counterpart). Most are imported by their human-readable name or slug — a UUID is always accepted too:  terraform import devhelm_monitor.api_health "API Health"  terraform import devhelm_alert_channel.ops_slack "Engineering Slack"  terraform import devhelm_tag.production "production"   See Importing resources for the full ID table.  ​ When to use Terraform vs YAML  Use case Recommended tool Monitors managed alongside cloud infra (AWS, GCP, etc.) Terraform provider Standalone monitoring config, fast iteration devhelm.yml + CLI CI/CD with GitHub Action devhelm.yml + setup-devhelm action Mixed infra — some Terraform, some standalone Use both (avoid managing the same resource in both)  Don’t manage the same resource with both Terraform and devhelm.yml . Pick one source of truth per resource to avoid drift and conflicts.  ​ Next steps  Terraform monitors Full devhelm_monitor resource reference. Alert channels Channel-type-specific arguments. Importing resources Import existing resources into Terraform state. Terraform in CI/CD Automate Terraform plans and applies in CI. Install it via npm and authenticate with an API token.  ​ Install  npm install -g devhelm   Verify the installation:  devhelm --version   ​ Authentication  The CLI resolves your API token from (in priority order):   --api-token flag on any command  DEVHELM_API_TOKEN environment variable  Saved context in ~/.devhelm/contexts.json   # Option A: environment variable (recommended for CI)  export DEVHELM_API_TOKEN = dh_live_xxxxxxxx   # Option B: interactive login (saves to contexts.json)  devhelm auth login   ​ Command reference  The CLI ships a wide command surface across resource topics, status pages, deploy/state, and auth. Every list/get command supports --output json for machine-readable output (deploy/validate use text|json instead — see those commands’ references).  ​ Config as Code  Command Description devhelm validate <file> Validate config file syntax offline devhelm plan -f <file> Preview changes without applying devhelm deploy -f <file> Apply config changes devhelm deploy --dry-run -f <file> Simulate deploy without applying devhelm deploy force-unlock Release a stuck deploy lock  ​ Monitors  Command Description devhelm monitors list List all monitors devhelm monitors get <id> Get monitor details devhelm monitors create Create a monitor devhelm monitors update <id> Update a monitor devhelm monitors delete <id> Delete a monitor devhelm monitors pause <id> Pause a monitor devhelm monitors resume <id> Resume a paused monitor devhelm monitors test <id> Run an on-demand check devhelm monitors results <id> Show recent check results devhelm monitors set-channels <id> Replace a monitor’s alert channel links devhelm monitors versions list <id> List monitor config versions  ​ Incidents  Command Description devhelm incidents list List incidents devhelm incidents get <id> Get incident details devhelm incidents create Create a manual incident devhelm incidents resolve <id> Resolve an incident  ​ Alert channels  Command Description devhelm alert-channels list List alert channels devhelm alert-channels get <id> Get channel details devhelm alert-channels create Create an alert channel devhelm alert-channels update <id> Update a channel devhelm alert-channels delete <id> Delete a channel devhelm alert-channels test <id> Send a test notification  ​ Other resources  Topic Commands notification-policies list, get, create, update, delete tags list, get, create, update, delete title: TypeScript SDK - DevHelm
text:
Documentation Index Fetch the complete documentation index at:  /llms.txt Use this file to discover all available pages before exploring further. Skip to main content DevHelm home page Search... ⌘ K Home Dashboard Dashboard Search... Navigation TypeScript SDK TypeScript SDK Docs Guides Integrations API Reference CLI Monitoring as Code SDKs Learn Overview Overview TypeScript SDK Quickstart Client Reference Error Handling Pagination Python SDK Quickstart Client Reference Error Handling Async Usage MCP Server Overview Tools Reference Configuration AI Skills Overview Configuration Examples On this page Install Initialize Create a monitor List monitors Update or delete a monitor Get check results Manage incidents Create an alert channel Error handling Resource namespaces Next steps TypeScript SDK TypeScript SDK Copy page Copy page Install and use the DevHelm TypeScript SDK to manage monitors, incidents, and alerts programmatically Copy page Copy page The @devhelm/sdk package is a typed, promise-based client for the DevHelm REST API. It runs in any modern Node.js or browser environment, ships full TypeScript types, and uses Zod for runtime request/response validation.  ​ Install  npm install @devhelm/sdk   Requires Node 18+ (for native fetch ).  ​ Initialize  import { Devhelm } from "@devhelm/sdk" ;   const client = new Devhelm ({  token: process . env . DEVHELM_API_TOKEN ! ,  });   Option Type Default Description token string — API token (Bearer). Required. baseUrl string https://api.devhelm.io Override for self-hosted or testing. orgId string DEVHELM_ORG_ID env or "1" Organization ID header. workspaceId string DEVHELM_WORKSPACE_ID when set Workspace ID header. Omit it when the organization has one workspace.  ​ Create a monitor  const monitor = await client . monitors . create ({  name: "API Health" ,  type: "HTTP" ,  config: {  url: "https://api.example.com/health" ,  method: "GET" ,  },  frequencySeconds: 60 ,  regions: [ "us-east" , "eu-west" ],  });   console . log ( `Created monitor: ${ monitor . id } ` );   managedBy is optional — omit it (defaults to API server-side) or set it
explicitly to one of API , DASHBOARD , CLI , TERRAFORM , or MCP to
record the provenance for drift detection.  Request bodies are validated against the generated Zod schemas before any HTTP I/O — invalid payloads throw DevhelmValidationError with structured field errors.  ​ List monitors  // Auto-paginates through every page  const monitors = await client . monitors . list ();   for ( const monitor of monitors ) {  console . log ( ` ${ monitor . name } : ${ monitor . currentStatus } ` );  }   For manual pagination control:  const page = await client . monitors . listPage ( 0 , 50 );  console . log ( `Total: ${ page . totalElements } ` );  for ( const monitor of page . data ) {  // ...  }   ​ Update or delete a monitor  // Update  const updated = await client . monitors . update ( monitor . id , {  frequencySeconds: 30 ,  });   // Delete  await client . monitors . delete ( monitor . id );   ​ Get check results  const results = await client . monitors . results ( monitor . id , { limit: 10 });   for ( const check of results . data ) {  const status = check . passed ? "OK" : "FAIL" ;  console . log ( ` ${ check . region } : ${ status } ( ${ check . responseTimeMs } ms)` );  }   // Fetch the next batch  if ( results . hasMore ) {  const next = await client . monitors . results ( monitor . id , {  cursor: results . nextCursor ! ,  limit: 10 ,  });  }   ​ Manage incidents  const incidents = await client . incidents . list ();   for ( const incident of incidents ) {  if ( incident . status === "OPEN" ) {  console . log ( `Open: ${ incident . title } ` );  }  }   await client . incidents . resolve ( incidentId );  // or with a resolution note:  await client . incidents . resolve ( incidentId , { body: "fixed by deploy" });   ​ Create an alert channel  const channel = await client . alertChannels . create ({  name: "Slack Alerts" ,  config: {  channelType: "slack" ,  webhookUrl: process . env . SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL ! ,  },  });   The channel type is the channelType discriminator inside  config ( slack , email , discord , pagerduty , …) — there is no top-level type field on this request.  ​ Error handling  import {  DevhelmError ,  DevhelmAuthError ,  DevhelmNotFoundError ,  DevhelmRateLimitError ,  } from "@devhelm/sdk" ;   try {  await client . monitors . get ( "nonexistent" );  } catch ( err ) {  if ( err instanceof DevhelmNotFoundError ) {  console . error ( "Monitor not found" );  } else if ( err instanceof DevhelmRateLimitError ) {  console . error ( `Rate limited (request_id= ${ err . requestId } )` );  } else if ( err instanceof DevhelmAuthError ) {  console . error ( "Bad token or insufficient permissions" );  } else if ( err instanceof DevhelmError ) {  throw err ;  }  }   Full taxonomy in the Error handling guide .  ​ Resource namespaces  The client exposes 19 resources:  Namespace Covers client.monitors HTTP, DNS, TCP, ICMP, MCP, Heartbeat monitors + check results, versions client.incidents Manual and auto-detected incidents client.forensics Incident timelines, check traces, policy snapshots, rule evaluations client.alertChannels Email, Slack, Discord, webhook, PagerDuty, OpsGenie, Teams client.notificationPolicies Routing rules, schedules client.environments Workspace environments (production, staging, …) client.secrets Secret values consumed by monitor configs client.tags Color-coded labels for monitors and incidents client.resourceGroups Compose monitors and dependencies into logical units client.webhooks Outbound event delivery client.inboxes Webhook testing inboxes: capture requests your code sends and wait for them client.email Email testing: per-test addresses, inject, wait, OTP codes and links client.apiKeys Token issuance and revocation client.dependencies Tracked third-party services for status pages client.services Third-party service status catalog (search, live status, uptime, incidents) client.deployLock Acquire / release / inspect the deploy lock client.maintenanceWindows Scheduled alert-suppression windows client.status Dashboard overview metrics client.statusPages Status pages, components, groups, incidents, subscribers, custom domains  ​ Next steps  Client reference Every method, signature, and return type. Error handling Exception classes and retry patterns. Webhook inboxes Assert on the webhooks your code sends with client.inboxes . Email testing Wait for sign-up and reset emails with client.email . title: Python SDK - DevHelm
text:
Documentation Index Fetch the complete documentation index at:  /llms.txt Use this file to discover all available pages before exploring further. Skip to main content DevHelm home page Search... ⌘ K Home Dashboard Dashboard Search... Navigation Python SDK Python SDK Docs Guides Integrations API Reference CLI Monitoring as Code SDKs Learn Overview Overview TypeScript SDK Quickstart Client Reference Error Handling Pagination Python SDK Quickstart Client Reference Error Handling Async Usage MCP Server Overview Tools Reference Configuration AI Skills Overview Configuration Examples On this page Install Initialize Create a monitor List monitors Get check results Manage incidents Create an alert channel Error handling Next steps Python SDK Python SDK Copy page Copy page Install and use the DevHelm Python SDK to manage monitors, incidents, and alerts programmatically Copy page Copy page The devhelm Python package is a typed, synchronous client for the DevHelm REST API. It’s built on httpx , ships full Pydantic models for every request and response, and has full mypy strict-mode type coverage.  The Python SDK is synchronous . There’s no AsyncDevhelm client as of v1.10.0 — for concurrent usage, run the sync client in a thread pool (see async usage ).  ​ Install  pip install devhelm   Requires Python 3.11 or later.  ​ Initialize  import os  from devhelm import Devhelm   client = Devhelm( token = os.environ[ "DEVHELM_API_TOKEN" ])   Constructor parameter Type Default Description token str "" API token. Falls back to the DEVHELM_API_TOKEN env var when empty. base_url str https://api.devhelm.io API base URL — override for self-hosted. org_id str | None None Sets x-phelm-org-id header. Falls back to DEVHELM_ORG_ID env var, then "1" . workspace_id str | None None Sets x-phelm-workspace-id when set or when DEVHELM_WORKSPACE_ID is set. Omit it when the organization has one workspace. timeout float 30.0 Per-request timeout in seconds.  ​ Create a monitor  The SDK accepts request bodies as plain dicts (validated against the Pydantic request model) or as Pydantic instances. Both produce the same MonitorDto response:  monitor = client.monitors.create({  "name" : "API Health" ,  "type" : "HTTP" ,  "config" : { "url" : "https://api.example.com/health" , "method" : "GET" },  "frequencySeconds" : 60 ,  "regions" : [ "us-east" , "eu-west" ],  })   print ( f "Created monitor: { monitor.id } " )   managedBy is optional — omit it (defaults to API server-side) or set it
explicitly to one of API , DASHBOARD , CLI , TERRAFORM , or MCP to
record the provenance for drift detection.  Or validate into the typed request class first, which raises before any network call:  from devhelm import CreateMonitorRequest   request = CreateMonitorRequest.model_validate({  "name" : "API Health" ,  "type" : "HTTP" ,  "config" : { "url" : "https://api.example.com/health" , "method" : "GET" },  "frequencySeconds" : 60 ,  })  monitor = client.monitors.create(request)   ​ List monitors  monitors = client.monitors.list() # auto-paginates through every page   for monitor in monitors:  print ( f " { monitor.name } : { monitor.current_status } " )   For manual pagination control:  page = client.monitors.list_page( page = 0 , size = 50 )  print ( f "Total: { page.total_elements } " )  for monitor in page.data:  ...   ​ Get check results  results = client.monitors.results(monitor.id, limit = 10 )   for check in results.data:  status = "OK" if check.passed else "FAIL"  print ( f " { check.region } : { status } ( { check.response_time_ms } ms)" )   results() returns a CursorPage — call it with cursor=results.next_cursor to fetch the next batch.  ​ Manage incidents  incidents = client.incidents.list() # auto-paginates   for incident in incidents:  if incident.status == "OPEN" :  print ( f "Open: { incident.title } " )   client.incidents.resolve( str (incident.id))  # or with a resolution note:  client.incidents.resolve( str (incident.id), { "body" : "fixed by deploy" })   ​ Create an alert channel  channel = client.alert_channels.create({  "name" : "Slack Alerts" ,  "config" : {  "channelType" : "slack" ,  "webhookUrl" : os.environ[ "SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL" ],  },  })   The channel type is the channelType discriminator inside  config ( slack , email , discord , pagerduty , …) — there is no top-level type field on this request.  ​ Error handling  from devhelm import (  Devhelm,  DevhelmApiError,  DevhelmAuthError,  DevhelmNotFoundError,  DevhelmRateLimitError,  )   try :  client.monitors.get( "nonexistent-id" )  except DevhelmNotFoundError:  print ( "Monitor not found" )  except DevhelmRateLimitError as e:  print ( f "Rate limited (request_id= { e.request_id } ) — back off and retry" )  except DevhelmAuthError:  print ( "Bad token or insufficient permissions" )  except DevhelmApiError as e:  print ( f " { e.status } : { e.message } " )   Full taxonomy in the Error handling guide .  ​ Next steps  Client reference Every resource and method available on the client. Concurrency patterns Run the sync client concurrently with thread pools and asyncio. Webhook inboxes Assert on the webhooks your code sends with client.inboxes . Email testing Wait for sign-up and reset emails with client.email . text: DevHelm .io Product Uptime Monitoring HTTP, TCP, DNS, ICMP, MCP checks from 4 global regions with 30s intervals Browser Testing Beta Run Playwright checks for your critical browser journeys Dependency Intelligence Track 80+ external services, automatic correlation with your monitors Status Pages Branded, real-time status pages on your domain — included from the free tier Pricing Blog Docs Log in Start Free Start Free Privacy Policy How we handle your data. Introduction  This Privacy Policy describes how DevHelm ("we", "our", "us") collects, uses, and protects your personal information when you use our uptime monitoring platform and related services.  By using DevHelm, you agree to the collection and use of information in accordance with this policy.  Data Controller  DevHelm is operated by Vladyslav Mokrousov, sole proprietor (jednoosobowa działalność gospodarcza) registered in Poland, NIP: 8522710570. As the data controller, we determine the purposes and means of processing your personal data.  Information We Collect  Account Information  When you create an account, we collect your name, email address, and organization details. If you subscribe to a paid plan, payment processing is handled by our payment provider (Paddle) — we do not store your credit card details directly.  Monitoring Data  We collect and store the results of uptime checks you configure, including response times, status codes, and assertion results. This data is used to provide the monitoring service, generate alerts, and populate dashboards and status pages.  Usage Data  We collect information about how you interact with our platform, including pages visited, features used, and API calls made. This helps us improve the product and troubleshoot issues.  Log Data  Our servers automatically log information such as your IP address, browser type, and request timestamps. This data is retained for security and operational purposes.  Phone Numbers (SMS and Voice Alerts)  If you configure SMS or phone-call alert channels, we collect the phone numbers you provide, verification status (including one-time password confirmation), delivery metadata, and opt-out status. Phone numbers are used only to deliver the transactional alerts you configured and to honor carrier opt-out requests.  How We Use Your Information   Providing the Service: Running uptime checks, generating alerts, and displaying monitoring dashboards.  Communication: Sending alerts and incident notifications via email, SMS, voice call, and other channels you configure, plus essential service updates.  Improvement: Analyzing usage patterns to improve product features and user experience.  Security: Detecting and preventing abuse, fraud, and unauthorized access.  Support: Responding to your support requests and troubleshooting issues.   SMS and Phone Alerts  To enroll in DevHelm SMS alerts, a DevHelm account user adds a mobile number they control to an SMS alert channel, actively checks a dedicated SMS consent checkbox that is unchecked by default, and completes one-time password (OTP) verification. SMS alerts are not enabled until both affirmative consent and phone verification are complete.  After enrolling, you may receive recurring transactional SMS messages from DevHelm about monitoring incidents affecting services in your workspace (for example, downtime, acknowledgement, resolve, and reopen notifications), as well as user-requested channel test messages. If you separately configure a phone-call alert channel, DevHelm may place automated calls about the same incidents and channel tests to the verified number.  Message frequency varies with incident activity and is limited by your plan's SMS and call allowances. Message and data rates may apply.  You may opt out of SMS alerts at any time by replying STOP to any DevHelm SMS message. After you opt out, we will send a confirmation and will not send further alert SMS to that number until you opt back in (for example by replying START ) or re-verify the number in the dashboard. Reply HELP for assistance, or contact support@devhelm.io .  We do not share, sell, or provide your mobile phone number or messaging consent data to third parties or affiliates for marketing or promotional purposes. Text messaging originator opt-in data and consent will not be sold, rented, transferred, or shared with any third parties. Twilio processes mobile phone numbers on DevHelm's behalf solely to deliver the alerts you requested, process STOP/HELP/START commands, and report delivery status.  We do not use SMS or voice alert channels for marketing or promotional campaigns.  Data Storage and Security  All monitoring data is stored in US-based datacenters. Data is encrypted at rest and in transit. Secret credentials (such as webhook URLs and integration tokens) are encrypted with AES-256 and stored in a secure vault.  GDPR-compliant data handling for EU customers is possible. Contact us at privacy@devhelm.io for details.  Data Retention  Monitoring data retention depends on your plan tier. When you delete your account, we remove your personal data within 30 days, except where required by law. Phone numbers associated with alert channels and opt-out records are retained while needed to provide the Service and honor carrier opt-out obligations, then deleted with your account data subject to the same timeline.  Third-Party Services  We use the following third-party services:   Auth0 for authentication  Paddle for payment processing  DigitalOcean and AWS for infrastructure  Twilio for SMS delivery, voice calls, and phone-number verification (OTP)   Each of these services has their own privacy policy governing how they handle your data.  Your Rights  You have the right to:   Access your personal data  Correct inaccurate data  Request deletion of your data  Export your data  Withdraw consent for optional data processing, including SMS and voice alerts (via STOP, dashboard channel removal, or contacting us)   To exercise any of these rights, contact us at privacy@devhelm.io .  Changes to This Policy  We may update this Privacy Policy from time to time. We will notify you of significant changes via email or an in-app notification.  Contact Us  If you have questions about this Privacy Policy, contact us at privacy@devhelm.io . title: Devtool Telemetry — DevHelm
text: DevHelm .io Product Uptime Monitoring HTTP, TCP, DNS, ICMP, MCP checks from 4 global regions with 30s intervals Browser Testing Beta Run Playwright checks for your critical browser journeys Dependency Intelligence Track 80+ external services, automatic correlation with your monitors Status Pages Branded, real-time status pages on your domain — included from the free tier Pricing Blog Docs Log in Start Free Start Free Devtool Telemetry What our CLI, Terraform provider, MCP server, and SDKs report back — and how to turn it off. TL;DR  Our official devtools (CLI, Terraform provider, MCP server, JavaScript SDK, Python SDK) attach a few metadata headers to every authenticated API call. We use those headers to count how many organizations adopt each devtool and which versions are in active use. We never see your commands, monitor names, or any payload contents — only the fact that some call happened, plus the version of the client that made it.  If you'd rather we didn't collect even that, every devtool honors a single opt-out toggle (see Opting out below).  Why we collect this  DevHelm offers five distinct ways to interact with the platform: a web dashboard, a CLI, a Terraform provider, an MCP server (for Cursor / Claude Desktop / etc.), and SDKs in two languages. Without basic adoption signals from those clients, we can't answer questions like:   Is anybody using the Terraform provider? (decides whether we keep investing in it)  Can we deprecate CLI v0.5 yet? (decides our backward-compat burden)  Which MCP clients should we test against? (Cursor, Claude Desktop, others?)   The alternative — flying blind and either over- or under-investing in each surface — is worse for both us and you.  Exactly what we collect  Every authenticated request from an official DevHelm devtool carries these HTTP headers:  Header Example Notes X-DevHelm-Surface cli One of: cli , tf , mcp , sdk-js , sdk-py X-DevHelm-Surface-Version 0.7.2 Semver of the client binary / package  Surface-specific extras:  Header Sent by Example X-DevHelm-Cli-Os CLI darwin-arm64 , linux-x86_64 X-DevHelm-Cli-Install-Source CLI npm , brew , other X-DevHelm-Mcp-Client MCP server cursor , claude-desktop , claude-code , zed , vscode , windsurf X-DevHelm-Sdk-Name SDKs sdk-js , sdk-py  That's the complete list. Nothing about which command you ran, which monitor you queried, which keys you used, what hostnames you target, or the contents of any request body or response.  What we don't collect  For absolute clarity:   No command names or arguments.  devhelm monitors create --url https://acme.example arrives at our API as the same anonymous metadata as devhelm --version .  No request or response payloads. Our standard API audit log captures what changed in your account (because that's table stakes for any B2B platform), but the telemetry layer described here adds no extra payload visibility.  No source IPs in the telemetry rollup. (Source IP exists in our standard request logs for security and rate-limiting, governed by our Privacy Policy .)  No environment variables, file contents, or working directory from your machine.  No identifiers from your dev environment (no MAC addresses, no machine fingerprints).   What we do with it  The data lives in two places:   A single Postgres row per (organization × devtool) that holds: when we first saw the org on that surface, when we last saw it, a running count of calls, and the latest version observed. That's it. No per-call history.  Two PostHog events per (organization × devtool), ever : one when we first see the org on a given surface ( cli_first_run , tf_provider_first_apply , mcp_server_first_call , sdk_first_authenticated_request ) and — if we ever ship it — one if the org makes a call after a long dormancy. Sparse by design; not one event per API request.   Aggregate numbers from these signals show up in our internal GTM dashboards. They are never sold, never shared with marketing networks, and never used to build per-user profiles. They exist solely to inform DevHelm's own product investment and deprecation decisions.  Opting out  Set the DEVHELM_TELEMETRY=0 environment variable. Every official devtool reads this and, when set, simply does not send the surface headers. The API has no way to record what it doesn't receive.  The CLI also accepts a per-invocation --no-telemetry flag for one-off opt-outs.  There is no separate "opt out via web settings" toggle — the headers are emitted by your local devtool, so the opt-out lives there. We deliberately built it this way so you don't have to trust a server-side setting.  Third-party / unofficial clients  If you call the DevHelm API directly with curl , your own scripts, or an unofficial client, you naturally do not send these headers and we collect nothing surface-related. That path is fully supported and not penalized.  Changes  This page is the source of truth. We will update it before changing what the official devtools collect, never after. The history is visible in the devhelmhq/mono repo.  Last updated: May 2026. Navigation Synthetics Synthetics Docs Guides Integrations API Reference CLI Monitoring as Code SDKs Learn Getting Started Introduction Quickstart Authentication Testing Webhook inboxes Email testing Security and data Limits and errors Monitoring as Code Monitoring as Code Monitoring Overview HTTP Monitors TCP Monitors DNS Monitors ICMP Monitors MCP Server Monitors Heartbeat Monitors Regions Check Results Synthetics Overview API checks Incidents Overview Policies Manual Incidents Maintenance Windows Timeline Forensics Alerting Overview Channels Notification Policies Escalation Chains Suppression Status Data Overview Services Dependencies Incidents Uptime Platform Environments Tags Secrets API Keys Resource Groups Common Patterns Pagination Errors Rate Limits Troubleshooting On this page Choose a check type Prepare the test package Configure the schedule Read a failed run Keep revisions reproducible Synthetics Synthetics Copy page Copy page Run packaged Playwright browser journeys and multi-step API checks, then inspect their run history and captured evidence Copy page Copy page Use Synthetics to check a complete browser journey or a sequence of API requests. A monitor runs a packaged Playwright test on a schedule, in the regions you select. Open its run history in the dashboard to investigate failures.  ​ Choose a check type  Type Use it for Browser Sign-in, signup, checkout, and other journeys that need a browser Multi-step API Authenticate, create a resource, read it back, and clean up without opening a browser  A browser check uses the BROWSER monitor type. A multi-step API check uses MULTI_STEP_API . Your test code contains the assertions; these monitor types do not use the assertion editor for HTTP uptime monitors.  ​ Prepare the test package  Keep the test and the local files it imports together in a ZIP. Choose the entrypoint by its relative path inside the archive, such as tests/checkout.spec.ts . Record the SHA-256 digest of the ZIP and the list of included files.  Keep credentials out of the package. Associate the monitor with an environment, declare the secret names the test requires, and configure their bindings. The test reads its runtime variables through process.env .  Package creation currently uses the API. The dashboard provides monitor
settings, bindings, revisions, and run evidence; it does not provide a ZIP
upload wizard. The published CLI does not expose a Synthetics package upload
command.  Follow the package creation workflow . Browser checks use the same workflow with type set to BROWSER and a browser test entrypoint.  ​ Configure the schedule  Set the check frequency and selected regions when creating the monitor. You can inspect and change the schedule in the monitor’s settings. Available regions and minimum intervals depend on your deployment and plan; see probe regions and the workspace’s current limits.  Each selected region performs its own run. Increasing the number of regions or shortening the interval increases run usage. Browser and API checks use separate run allowances.  ​ Read a failed run  Open Synthetics , select the monitor, and open a run from its history. The run identifies its region, outcome, duration, and revision. Use the steps and evidence views to inspect the failure.  Browser evidence can include screenshots, video, a trace, network requests, console output, and runner logs. What is available depends on what the run captured and whether the artifact is still retained. The viewer distinguishes available, missing, and expired artifacts.  An API check reports its test outcome and recorded evidence. It does not produce browser screenshots or video. Put meaningful assertions and cleanup in the test so a failure identifies the request or condition that broke.  Run now starts an actual run and consumes usage. The uptime monitor’s
synchronous Test action is not available for Browser or Multi-step API
monitors.  ​ Keep revisions reproducible  A package revision records its digest, entrypoint, and file list. Optional Git metadata records which commit produced it. Runs retain their revision reference, so you can compare failures without assuming they used the latest uploaded files.  Multi-step API checks Package a request sequence and create its monitor through the API. API authentication Create a token for the workspace that owns your checks. Navigation Synthetics Multi-step API checks Docs Guides Integrations API Reference CLI Monitoring as Code SDKs Learn Getting Started Introduction Quickstart Authentication Testing Webhook inboxes Email testing Security and data Limits and errors Monitoring as Code Monitoring as Code Monitoring Overview HTTP Monitors TCP Monitors DNS Monitors ICMP Monitors MCP Server Monitors Heartbeat Monitors Regions Check Results Synthetics Overview API checks Incidents Overview Policies Manual Incidents Maintenance Windows Timeline Forensics Alerting Overview Channels Notification Policies Escalation Chains Suppression Status Data Overview Services Dependencies Incidents Uptime Platform Environments Tags Secrets API Keys Resource Groups Common Patterns Pagination Errors Rate Limits Troubleshooting On this page Prepare your package Upload and create the monitor Request an upload URL Create the monitor Inspect the result Update the test Synthetics Multi-step API checks Copy page Copy page Package a Playwright request sequence and create a scheduled Multi-step API monitor using the published API Copy page Copy page Use a multi-step API check when availability depends on several requests succeeding together. A token endpoint returning 200 does not prove that a caller can create an invoice and read it back.  Write the sequence as a Playwright test that uses the request fixture. Assert the expected response at each step and clean up resources your test creates. Use test accounts and data suitable for repeated execution against the target environment.  ​ Prepare your package  Put the test entrypoint and the local files it imports in a ZIP. Paths in the package metadata are relative to the archive root: tests/invoice.spec.ts identifies that file inside the ZIP, not an absolute path on your computer.  You need:   The ZIP’s SHA-256 digest, as 64 hexadecimal characters  The entrypoint path and included file paths  An environment ID in the monitor’s workspace  Any secret names the package requires and their environment bindings   Do not include credentials in the ZIP. Set sensitive values through your environment’s secret bindings and read them from process.env in the test.  ​ Upload and create the monitor  Authenticate with a token that can write monitors in the selected workspace. Set DEVHELM_API_TOKEN , DEVHELM_WORKSPACE_ID , ENVIRONMENT_ID , and PACKAGE_SHA256 before running the examples. PACKAGE_SHA256 must match the exact ZIP bytes you upload.  ​ Request an upload URL  API curl -sS -X POST "https://api.devhelm.io/api/v1/monitors/package-uploads" \  -H "Authorization: Bearer $DEVHELM_API_TOKEN " \  -H "x-phelm-workspace-id: $DEVHELM_WORKSPACE_ID " \  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \  -d "{ \" digest \" : \" $PACKAGE_SHA256 \" }"   The response contains putUrl , expiresAt , and requiredHeaders . Upload the ZIP bytes with HTTP PUT to that signed URL before it expires. Send the returned required headers, including Content-Type: application/zip and If-None-Match: * .  The signed storage URL authorizes the upload. Do not send your DevHelm API token to it. If the same digest already exists, preserve the existing object; changing the package requires a new digest.  ​ Create the monitor  After the upload succeeds, create a MULTI_STEP_API monitor that references the package metadata:  API curl -sS -X POST "https://api.devhelm.io/api/v1/monitors" \  -H "Authorization: Bearer $DEVHELM_API_TOKEN " \  -H "x-phelm-workspace-id: $DEVHELM_WORKSPACE_ID " \  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \  -d "{ \" name \" : \" invoice-roundtrip \" , \" type \" : \" MULTI_STEP_API \" , \" environmentId \" : \" $ENVIRONMENT_ID \" , \" config \" :{ \" timeoutSeconds \" :30}, \" frequencySeconds \" :3600, \" regions \" :[ \" us-east \" ], \" package \" :{ \" digest \" : \" $PACKAGE_SHA256 \" , \" entrypoint \" : \" tests/invoice.spec.ts \" , \" files \" :[ \" tests/invoice.spec.ts \" ]}}"   The example assumes the ZIP contains one file, tests/invoice.spec.ts . Include every packaged local file in files . If the test requires secrets, also include their names in package.keys and configure the corresponding bindings.  The minimum frequency and run allowance depend on your plan. The example uses a one-hour interval; check the workspace’s limits before selecting a faster schedule or additional regions.  Do not send an inline config.script or HTTP-monitor assertion objects for a
code monitor. The package contains the test and its assertions. An environment
is required.  ​ Inspect the result  Open the monitor in the dashboard and inspect its run history. A failed request or assertion makes the test fail. Review the recorded evidence and runner output to understand which condition was not met.  Run now is a real run, with normal usage accounting. The synchronous uptime-monitor Test action is not supported for this check type.  ​ Update the test  Package the changed files and compute the new ZIP digest. Request a signed upload URL and upload those bytes before updating the monitor’s package metadata. Keep the entrypoint, file list, and optional Git attribution aligned with the uploaded revision. title: Who Monitors the Monitors? — DevHelm
text: DevHelm .io Product Uptime Monitoring HTTP, TCP, DNS, ICMP, MCP checks from 4 global regions with 30s intervals Browser Testing Beta Run Playwright checks for your critical browser journeys Dependency Intelligence Track 80+ external services, automatic correlation with your monitors Status Pages Branded, real-time status pages on your domain — included from the free tier Pricing Blog Docs Log in Start Free Start Free Blog Reliability Infrastructure Who Monitors the Monitors? Vladyslav / Aug 18, 2026 / 5 min read Sentry sells uptime monitoring. So who monitors Sentry?  Sentry's official status hostname is status.sentry.io . It lists incidents affecting the API and error ingestion. That page is not Sentry's origin: DNS shows it pointing at an Atlassian Statuspage customer hostname.  Even companies that sell monitoring use an independent system to expose their own availability. A status surface is only useful if it can still report an outage when the product it describes is unavailable.  We keep a separate record at devhelm.io/status/sentry , from probes that do not share Sentry's infrastructure.  The question, then, is not "why doesn't Sentry monitor itself?" It is why any uptime monitoring system should depend entirely on the infrastructure it is supposed to watch.  Why independent uptime monitoring exists  When the watcher shares fate with the thing being watched, one outage can take both down. The app stops responding, the status URL fails with it, and alerting never fires because it lived on the same path. Customers refresh a blank tab and search "is it down."  Independent uptime monitoring is the same idea applied to your product: scheduled probes from networks you do not control, against the URL your users actually hit, rather than a dashboard in the VPC or a health endpoint only your load balancer can see.  Other uptime tools do a version of the same pattern: branded status.* hostnames on infrastructure they do not operate. Get posts like this in your inbox Engineering insights on monitoring, incidents, and uptime. Bi-weekly, 2-minute read. Join free Status pages do not probe your origin  A hosted status page does not hit your production URL on a schedule. Graphs and automatic component flips need an external monitor or a custom integration. The page is a communications surface. Someone else has to do the checking, or an engineer types the incident by hand.  That is why hosting the board elsewhere is a resilience choice, not a gap. If the product is degraded, a status page on the same stack is often the first thing customers cannot load. The status page guide covers how to structure components and incidents. The constraint is simple: the page that says you are down should not go down with you.  An independent check can feed a status page. The page cannot stand in for the check.  Most uptime tools run their own probes and only borrow the status-page layer. A few put the public check UI on another vendor. They still keep the public notice board off the app.  Two separations  Mixing "who hosts the status page" with "who runs the probe" produces the wrong purchase.  First, separate your application from the thing that watches it. Internal health endpoints, APM, and error trackers (Sentry included) are necessary, and they share your runtime. A load balancer can show healthy pods while the public hostname returns 502. External checks exist for that class of failure. For SSL expiry, DNS cutovers, and regional probes, use the uptime guide .  Second, if you need to read "the vendor is down" during a vendor outage, their public status has to sit outside that vendor's product. Sentry's official status.sentry.io hostname is the public example.  For your product, the vendor-status hostname is optional. The external probe is required. If your only signal is a dashboard inside the same cluster as the app, you will learn about edge and DNS failures from a customer email.  The question to ask  Most vendors can monitor themselves, and do.  Ask whether the observer you are buying sits outside your infrastructure: a different network, DNS, cloud account, and deploy. Ask, separately, whether their public status page would still load if their app did not.  Keep the traces and the error tracker. Add an external probe on the user path. Keep the status page somewhere that is not the origin it describes.  See how we keep probes independent of the control plane at devhelm.io/reliability . title: End-to-End Synthetic Monitoring: HTTP Checks, JS Rendering, and Browser Journeys — DevHelm
text:
DevHelm .io Product Uptime Monitoring HTTP, TCP, DNS, ICMP, MCP checks from 4 global regions with 30s intervals Browser Testing Beta Run Playwright checks for your critical browser journeys Dependency Intelligence Track 80+ external services, automatic correlation with your monitors Status Pages Branded, real-time status pages on your domain — included from the free tier Pricing Blog Docs Log in Start Free Start Free Blog Guides Reliability Synthetic Monitoring End-to-End Synthetic Monitoring: HTTP Checks, JS Rendering, and Browser Journeys DevHelm Team / Jul 18, 2026 / 17 min read Synthetic monitoring is simple in theory: run scripted checks against production on a schedule so you learn about broken paths before customers do. In practice, most teams stop at HTTP 200 and call it done. End-to-end monitoring means stacking layers: probe the wire, inspect what the HTML actually contains, and only then escalate to a real browser when the user journey depends on JavaScript.  This guide builds that stack with runnable Python. You will probe five public targets, classify which of them are static HTML versus JS shells, scrape blog titles from a live SSR listing, prove why an empty SPA root fools a status check, and know when to hand off to a browser journey. For the category definition and tool comparison, start with what synthetic monitoring is and the 2026 tools roundup . This page is the how-to.  Prerequisites   Python 3.11+ with a virtualenv  httpx (or requests ) and beautifulsoup4 for Layer A/B  Optional: Playwright Python + Chromium for the Layer C snippet ( Playwright setup )  No paid accounts. All targets below are public.   python -m venv .venv # Windows: .venvScriptsactivate  # macOS/Linux: source .venv/bin/activate  pip install httpx beautifulsoup4 # optional later:  # pip install playwright && playwright install chromium  Create a working directory and keep each script as its own file so you can promote them into CI one layer at a time.  The three layers of an end-to-end check  Layer What it runs Catches Misses Relative cost A. HTTP / API GET/POST, assert status, headers, body, latency Outages, TLS failures, empty/wrong payloads, slow APIs Dead buttons, broken client JS, post-login UI Cheap B. Rendered HTML Parse HTML after fetch, or after a headless render Missing listing cards, wrong titles, SPA shells with no content Multi-step clicks, auth redirects, canvas/WebGL Medium C. Browser journey Headless Chromium through login/checkout The failures users actually hit Nothing Layer A/B already covered, if you over-use it Expensive  End-to-end monitoring (sometimes called e2e monitoring) is not "run Playwright on everything." It is matching the layer to the failure mode. API and uptime checks give you breadth. Browser checks give you depth on the few journeys that pay the bills. Headless browser monitoring is Layer C specifically; this guide starts at Layer A so you do not pay browser prices for problems a JSON assert would catch.  A useful rule of thumb: if a failure would show up in curl with a clear status or body problem, keep it on Layer A. If the failure only appears after the client bundle runs, you need Layer B or C. Get posts like this in your inbox Engineering insights on monitoring, incidents, and uptime. Bi-weekly, 2-minute read. Join free Layer A: Probe five public domains with HTTP  Pick targets that exercise different response shapes. The set below is deliberate:   https://example.com — tiny static HTML document  https://github.com — large application HTML  https://www.ft.com — often bot-gated (403 from datacenter IPs)  https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Page — server-rendered encyclopedia HTML  https://httpbin.org/get — JSON API, not a page   # probe_http.py  from __future__ import annotations  import time from dataclasses import dataclass  import httpx  TARGETS =  [   "https://example.com" ,   "https://github.com" ,   "https://www.ft.com" ,   "https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Page" ,   "https://httpbin.org/get" ,  ]   HEADERS =  {   "User-Agent" :  "DevHelmSyntheticGuide/1.0 (+https://devhelm.io/blog)" ,   "Accept" :  "text/html,application/json;q=0.9,*/*;q=0.8" ,  }    @dataclass  class  ProbeResult :  url :  str  status :  int  |  None  elapsed_ms :  int  content_type :  str  body_len :  int  error :  str  |  None  =  None    def  probe ( url :  str , client : httpx . Client )  - > ProbeResult :  started = time . perf_counter ( )   try :  response = client . get ( url , follow_redirects = True )  elapsed_ms =  int ( ( time . perf_counter ( )  - started )  *  1000 )   return ProbeResult (  url = url ,  status = response . status_code ,  elapsed_ms = elapsed_ms ,  content_type = response . headers . get ( "content-type" ,  "" ) ,  body_len = len ( response . content ) ,   )   except httpx . HTTPError as exc :  elapsed_ms =  int ( ( time . perf_counter ( )  - started )  *  1000 )   return ProbeResult (  url = url ,  status = None ,  elapsed_ms = elapsed_ms ,  content_type = "" ,  body_len = 0 ,  error = type ( exc ) . __name__ ,   )    def  main ( )  - >  None :   with httpx . Client ( headers = HEADERS , timeout = 20.0 )  as client :   for url in TARGETS :  result = probe ( url , client )   print (   f" { result . status !s : >4 }  { result . elapsed_ms : >5 } ms  "   f" { result . body_len : >7 } B { result . content_type [ : 40 ] : <40 } "   f" { result . error or  '' }  { result . url } "   )    if __name__ ==  "__main__" :  main ( )  Run it:  python probe_http.py  A representative run from typical cloud or datacenter egress looks like this (numbers move; the shapes matter):  200    120ms      648B  text/html                                https://example.com
 200    190ms   500000B+ text/html; charset=utf-8                 https://github.com
 403     80ms    12000B  text/html                                https://www.ft.com
 200    240ms   100000B+ text/html; charset=UTF-8                 https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Page
 200    500ms      300B  application/json                         https://httpbin.org/get  Three lessons show up immediately.  Status code is not the product.  example.com returning 200 with a few hundred bytes of HTML is fine. httpbin.org/get returning 200 with JSON is fine only if you assert a field (for example "url" present). GitHub returning 200 does not mean your authenticated dashboard works.  Bot and WAF responses are first-class signals.  ft.com returning 403 from many server IPs is not "the Financial Times is down." It is "this probe path is blocked." Synthetic monitoring from datacenters will see this class of result. Treat 403 and 429 as classified outcomes (expected for that target, or a CDN misconfig on your site), not as a binary up/down.  Latency budgets belong on the probe. A 200 that takes 8 seconds is an incident for many APIs. Record elapsed_ms next to status from day one. Persist the metric even when the assert passes so you can spot slow regressions before they turn into timeouts.  Assert on the body, not only the status  def  assert_httpbin ( response : httpx . Response )  - >  None :   assert response . status_code ==  200   assert  "application/json"  in response . headers . get ( "content-type" ,  "" )  payload = response . json ( )   assert payload . get ( "url" )  ==  "https://httpbin.org/get"   assert  "headers"  in payload  assert response . elapsed . total_seconds ( )  <  3.0    def  assert_example ( response : httpx . Response )  - >  None :   assert response . status_code ==  200  text = response . text  assert  "Example Domain"  in text  assert  len ( text )  >  100  Wire those asserts into the probe loop so a wrong body fails the process:  ASSERTIONS =  {   "https://example.com" : assert_example ,   "https://httpbin.org/get" : assert_httpbin ,  }   with httpx . Client ( headers = HEADERS , timeout = 20.0 )  as client :   for url , assert_fn in ASSERTIONS . items ( ) :  response = client . get ( url , follow_redirects = True )  assert_fn ( response )   print ( f"OK { url } " )  This is API synthetic monitoring in miniature: request, assert structure, fail closed. For how API testing in CI differs from production API monitoring, see API testing vs API monitoring .  Multi-step API checks (still Layer A)  Many "user journeys" are really sequences of HTTP calls. You can cover them without a browser:  def  assert_httpbin_flow ( client : httpx . Client )  - >  None :   # 1) Read a baseline payload  get_resp = client . get ( "https://httpbin.org/get" )   assert get_resp . status_code ==  200   assert get_resp . json ( ) [ "url" ] . endswith ( "/get" )    # 2) Echo a POST body (stand-in for "create resource")  post_resp = client . post (   "https://httpbin.org/post" ,  json = { "order_id" :  "synth-1" ,  "amount" :  19.0 } ,   )   assert post_resp . status_code ==  200  echoed = post_resp . json ( ) [ "json" ]   assert echoed [ "order_id" ]  ==  "synth-1"   assert echoed [ "amount" ]  ==  19.0  Against your own API the pattern is the same: authenticate, create, read back, delete, assert each step. That is end-to-end service monitoring at the protocol layer. Save the browser for steps that only exist in the DOM.  Detect JavaScript-rendered apps from the HTTP response  Many modern apps return HTTP 200 with almost no user-visible content until JavaScript runs. If your only check is status code, that shell looks healthy forever.  # classify_html.py  from __future__ import annotations  import re from dataclasses import dataclass  import httpx from bs4 import BeautifulSoup  HEADERS =  {   "User-Agent" :  "DevHelmSyntheticGuide/1.0 (+https://devhelm.io/blog)" ,  }    @dataclass  class  PageClass :  url :  str  status :  int  kind :  str  # static | spa_shell | api_json | blocked | unknown  reasons :  list [ str ]    def  classify ( url :  str , client : httpx . Client )  - > PageClass :  response = client . get ( url , follow_redirects = True )  ctype = response . headers . get ( "content-type" ,  "" )  reasons :  list [ str ]  =  [ ]    if response . status_code in  { 401 ,  403 ,  429 } :   return PageClass ( url , response . status_code ,  "blocked" ,  [ "non-2xx access control" ] )    if  "application/json"  in ctype :   return PageClass ( url , response . status_code ,  "api_json" ,  [ "content-type json" ] )   html = response . text soup = BeautifulSoup ( html ,  "html.parser" )   for tag in soup ( [ "script" ,  "style" ,  "noscript" ] ) :  tag . decompose ( )  visible = re . sub ( r"s+" ,  " " , soup . get_text ( " " , strip = True ) )   root = soup . find ( id = "root" )  or soup . find ( id = "app" )  or soup . find ( id = "__next" )   if root is  not  None  and  len ( visible )  <  80 :  reasons . append ( "mount point with almost no text" )   return PageClass ( url , response . status_code ,  "spa_shell" , reasons )    if  len ( visible )  <  80 :  reasons . append ( f"visible text only { len ( visible ) } chars" )   return PageClass ( url , response . status_code ,  "spa_shell" , reasons )    if  "enable javascript"  in visible . lower ( ) :  reasons . append ( "enable-javascript message" )   return PageClass ( url , response . status_code ,  "spa_shell" , reasons )   reasons . append ( f"visible text ~ { len ( visible ) } chars" )   return PageClass ( url , response . status_code ,  "static" , reasons )    URLS =  [   "https://example.com" ,   "https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Page" ,   "https://httpbin.org/get" ,   "https://www.ft.com" ,   "https://app.devhelm.io/login" ,  ]   if __name__ ==  "__main__" :   with httpx . Client ( headers = HEADERS , timeout = 20.0 )  as client :   for url in URLS :  result = classify ( url , client )   print (   f" { result . kind : <10 }  { result . status }  { result . url } "   f"( { '; ' . join ( result . reasons ) } )"   )  Expected shape of the output:  static     200  https://example.com  (visible text ~…)
static     200  https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Page  (visible text ~…)
api_json   200  https://httpbin.org/get  (content-type json)
blocked    403  https://www.ft.com  (non-2xx access control)
spa_shell  200  https://app.devhelm.io/login  (mount point with almost no text)  https://app.devhelm.io/login is the clean teaching case: status 200, an empty #root , and effectively zero visible text until the SPA boots. An HTTP-only uptime check on that URL will stay green while the login UI is broken. That gap is why browser synthetic monitoring exists.  Heuristics are not perfect. SSR frameworks (including Next.js) often ship full HTML in the first response even when they hydrate on the client. Classification tells you whether this URL is safe to trust from Layer A, not whether the product as a whole is an SPA.  When you classify a URL as spa_shell , do not "fix" the HTTP check by asserting on a script filename. Script tags can remain while the UI is blank. Move that URL's critical asserts to Layer C.  Layer B: Scrape blog titles from https://devhelm.io/blog  The DevHelm blog listing is server-rendered. Post titles appear as real <h2> elements inside links to /blog/<slug> in the first HTML response. That makes it a good Layer B exercise: prove your parser reads production content, not that the CDN returned a shell.  # scrape_blog.py  from __future__ import annotations  import httpx from bs4 import BeautifulSoup  BLOG_URL =  "https://devhelm.io/blog"  HEADERS =  {   "User-Agent" :  "DevHelmSyntheticGuide/1.0 (+https://devhelm.io/blog)" ,  }  MIN_POSTS =  15    def  scrape_titles ( html :  str )  - >  list [ str ] :  soup = BeautifulSoup ( html ,  "html.parser" )  titles :  list [ str ]  =  [ ]   for link in soup . select ( 'a[href^="/blog/"]' ) :  heading = link . find ( "h2" )   if heading is  None :   continue  text = heading . get_text ( strip = True )  href = link . get ( "href" )  or  ""   # Skip nav-only /blog links without a slug   if href . rstrip ( "/" )  ==  "/blog"  or  not text :   continue  titles . append ( text )   # de-dupe while preserving order  seen :  set [ str ]  =  set ( )  unique :  list [ str ]  =  [ ]   for title in titles :   if title in seen :   continue  seen . add ( title )  unique . append ( title )   return unique   def  main ( )  - >  None :   with httpx . Client ( headers = HEADERS , timeout = 20.0 )  as client :  response = client . get ( BLOG_URL , follow_redirects = True )   assert response . status_code ==  200 , response . status_code titles = scrape_titles ( response . text )   print ( f"Blog posts found: { len ( titles ) } " )   for title in titles [ : 5 ] :   print ( f"  - { title } " )   assert  len ( titles )  >= MIN_POSTS ,  f"expected >= { MIN_POSTS } , got { len ( titles ) } "   print ( f"OK: { len ( titles ) } >= { MIN_POSTS } " )    if __name__ ==  "__main__" :  main ( )  python scrape_blog.py  You should see a count around 20 (the listing grows over time; the floor assert keeps the check stable) and the first few titles printed. That is content assertion: the page is not merely reachable, it still exposes the listing cards you care about.  Use a floor ( >= 15 ), not an exact count. Exact equality breaks the first time you publish a new post. Floors catch "the listing disappeared" without paging you for growth.  Contrast: HTTP scrape versus browser render  For devhelm.io/blog , HTTP is enough because the titles are in the initial HTML. For app.devhelm.io/login , the same BeautifulSoup pass finds no usable login copy inside #root . The fix is not a smarter regex. The fix is Layer C: load the page in a browser, wait for the client render, then assert.  # render_spa_title.py  (optional; requires Playwright)  from playwright . sync_api import sync_playwright  URL =  "https://app.devhelm.io/login"   with sync_playwright ( )  as p :  browser = p . chromium . launch ( headless = True )  page = browser . new_page ( )  page . goto ( URL , wait_until = "domcontentloaded" )  page . locator ( "body" ) . wait_for ( state = "visible" )   # Prefer a role/label once the Auth0 (or app) UI paints  page . get_by_label ( "Email address" ) . wait_for ( state = "visible" , timeout = 30_000 )   print ( "rendered login email field: OK" )   print ( "title after render:" , page . title ( ) )  browser . close ( )  Keep this snippet short on purpose. Locators, codegen, traces, and a full Python Playwright path live in What Is Playwright? A Practical Guide . Turning an existing journey into a scheduled production check is covered in Playwright monitoring and browser monitoring with Playwright .  If you want a second render target that is not your own login page, https://demo.playwright.dev/todomvc is a public TodoMVC demo. The raw HTML is thin; after a browser load you can assert on the todo input. Same lesson, different site.  What to assert (beyond status codes)  End-to-end service monitoring fails when assertions are lazy. Use a short checklist per layer:  Layer A (HTTP/API)   Status in an allow-list (200, or 401 if you are probing that auth is required)  Content-Type matches the contract  JSON path or HTML substring that proves the payload is the real one  Latency under a budget (a goal you measure, not a hope)   Layer B (rendered listing / SSR page)   Element count floors ( >= 15 posts), not exact equality that breaks on every publish  Critical strings (product name, pricing number, "Order confirmed")  Canonical URL after redirects   Layer C (browser)   Visible control the user needs (email field, Pay button)  Post-action URL or heading  Screenshot or trace on failure for forensics   Also decide what not to alert on. A third-party 403 you classified as blocked should not wake the on-call. A 403 on your own checkout host should. Classification turns raw status codes into actionable signals.  Intervals, flaky selectors, and alert routing are a discipline of their own. Read synthetic monitoring best practices before you page humans on every blip.  Layer C: When you need a real browser journey  Escalate to a browser when the failure mode is client-side:   Login and SSO redirects  Checkout and payment iframes  Multi-step wizards that never hit a single JSON endpoint you own  "Button does nothing" bugs behind a green API   That class of work is synthetic transaction monitoring: a multi-step script that mimics a revenue or auth path. It is also where cost and maintenance jump. Prefer one solid checkout check over twenty brittle page opens.  You do not need a browser to know httpbin.org/get returned valid JSON. You do need a browser to know the login form on an empty #root SPA still accepts an email. Match the tool to the risk.  A practical promotion path for most teams:   Write the HTTP asserts for the APIs behind the journey.  Add an SSR/content scrape for any public listing that must stay populated.  Add one browser script for the money or auth path.  Schedule all three; alert on severity, not on every layer equally.   Synthetic monitoring and real-user monitoring answer different questions; run both when you can. The split is explained in synthetic monitoring vs RUM .  Put the layers in one runner  Once the pieces work, a single entrypoint makes CI and cron easier:  # main.py  from __future__ import annotations  import httpx  from classify_html import classify from scrape_blog import scrape_titles , BLOG_URL , MIN_POSTS , HEADERS  CRITICAL_HTTP =  [   "https://example.com" ,   "https://httpbin.org/get" ,   "https://devhelm.io/blog" ,  ]    def  main ( )  - >  None :   with httpx . Client ( headers = HEADERS , timeout = 20.0 )  as client :   for url in CRITICAL_HTTP :  response = client . get ( url , follow_redirects = True )   assert response . status_code ==  200 ,  f" { url } -> { response . status_code } "   print ( f"HTTP OK { url } " )   blog = client . get ( BLOG_URL , follow_redirects = True )  titles = scrape_titles ( blog . text )   assert  len ( titles )  >= MIN_POSTS  print ( f"Blog OK { len ( titles ) } titles" )   spa = classify ( "https://app.devhelm.io/login" , client )   assert spa . kind ==  "spa_shell"   print ( f"Classified login as { spa . kind } (browser layer required)" )    if __name__ ==  "__main__" :  main ( )  The last assert is intentional: you are documenting that login is not covered by HTTP. The runner stays green only if you still recognize the SPA shell. Separately, schedule the Playwright login check so the UI itself is watched.  Schedule the stack  A script on a laptop is a prototype. End-to-end monitoring means the same asserts run on a schedule, from somewhere outside your VPC, with an alert when they fail.  Minimal path:   Keep the probe and scrape scripts in git.  Run them in CI on a cron ( schedule: in GitHub Actions) or a system timer.  Exit non-zero on assert failure so the job is red.  Wire the failure to Slack, PagerDuty, or email.   # .github/workflows/synthetic-http.yml  name : Synthetic HTTP probes on :   schedule :   -  cron :  "*/15 * * * *"   workflow_dispatch :  jobs :   probe :   runs-on : ubuntu - latest  steps :   -  uses : actions/checkout@v4  -  uses : actions/setup - python@v5  with :   python-version :  "3.12"   -  run : pip install httpx beautifulsoup4  -  run : python main.py  That gets you Layer A/B from one region every 15 minutes. It does not replace multi-region product monitoring, private locations, or rich failure artifacts. Failures that only happen in one geography (bad DNS, expired edge cert, partial deploy) need probes in more than one place.  When cron is no longer enough, compare platforms in best synthetic monitoring tools and keep definitions in git via monitoring as code .  FAQ  What is end-to-end monitoring?  End-to-end monitoring (e2e monitoring) means verifying a path the way a user or dependent system experiences it: not only that a process is up, but that the request, response, and (when needed) rendered UI still satisfy the contract. In web systems that usually means HTTP asserts plus selective browser journeys.  Is synthetic monitoring the same thing?  Synthetic monitoring is the broader practice of generating scripted traffic on a schedule. End-to-end monitoring is the subset that follows a full path. A single /health ping is synthetic. A login-plus-dashboard check is synthetic and end-to-end.  Do I need Playwright for every check?  No. Use HTTP and API checks for breadth. Use a browser when the page is a JS shell or the journey is interactive. Over-using browsers creates flaky alerts and large bills.  Why did ft.com return 403?  Many publishers block datacenter and bot User-Agents. Your synthetic probes will see 403 and 429 on third-party sites. On your product, unexpected 403s are incidents; on someone else's site used as a teaching target, they are classification data.  How is this different from the Playwright guide?  The Playwright guide teaches the browser toolkit: Page API, locators, waits, codegen, login flows, CI. This guide teaches the monitoring stack around that toolkit: when HTTP is enough, how to detect JS shells, how to assert on SSR content, and when to promote a check to a browser. Read them as a pair.  What to do next   Put Layer A asserts on your real APIs and public pages (status, body, latency).  Classify each critical URL as static, API, or SPA shell before you buy browser minutes.  Add one Layer C journey for login or checkout; write it properly with the Playwright guide , then schedule it with Playwright monitoring .  Run multi-region HTTP and API monitors with body assertions at app.devhelm.io . First monitor is live in about a minute, no credit card.  On this page Prerequisites The three layers of an end-to-end check Layer A: Probe five public domains with HTTP Detect JavaScript-rendered apps from the HTTP response Layer B: Scrape blog titles from `https://devhelm.io/blog` What to assert (beyond status codes) Layer C: When you need a real browser journey Put the layers in one runner Schedule the stack FAQ What to do next Get posts like this in your inbox Engineering insights on monitoring, incidents, and uptime.
