title: Best Server Monitoring Tools in 2026: Host Metrics Without Buying the Wrong Stack — DevHelm
text: DevHelm .io Product Uptime Monitoring HTTP, TCP, DNS, ICMP, MCP checks from 4 global regions with 30s intervals Browser Testing Beta Run Playwright checks for your critical browser journeys Dependency Intelligence Track 80+ external services, automatic correlation with your monitors Status Pages Branded, real-time status pages on your domain — included from the free tier Pricing Blog Docs Log in Start Free Start Free Blog Comparisons Guides Best Server Monitoring Tools in 2026: Host Metrics Without Buying the Wrong Stack DevHelm Team / Jul 14, 2026 / 14 min read Host monitoring answers a narrow question: is this machine healthy? CPU, memory, disk, processes, and the alerts those signals should fire. That is a different purchase from endpoint uptime checks and from full APM. Mixing the three jobs is how teams buy a platform they underuse, or miss a full disk that never shows up in an HTTPS monitor.  Below we compare seven host and agent tools on how they collect data, how fine-grained the metrics are, what a roughly 50-host bill looks like, and how much ops work you take on. We are talking server-side collectors (agents, exporters, SNMP), not status-page or synthetic-journey products. Pricing checked July 2026. Related comparisons: cloud suites , open-source deploy complexity , website uptime .  External checks (not host agents)  DevHelm does not install a host agent. It watches HTTP, DNS, TCP, SSL, and heartbeats from outside your fleet and correlates failures with third-party status. Use it when the box looks fine but checkout is still red. Do not use it instead of CPU/RAM charts.  Free Starter Pro Price $0 $12/mo $29/mo Monitors 50 75 250 Interval 5 min 1 min 30 sec  Flat pricing, CLI/Terraform/SDK config, status page with custom domain on every tier. The rankings below are host collectors only.  Comparison at a glance  Tool Collects via Resolution Cost at about 50 hosts Ops load Datadog Vendor agent Near real-time About $15/host/mo Infra Pro (annual) + add-ons Low (SaaS) Prometheus + Grafana Exporters + scrape Often 15–60s $0 license; people + storage High Grafana Cloud Agent/Alloy → managed Prom Scrape interval $19/mo + active-series usage Low–medium Netdata Netdata agent Per-second 5 nodes free; Business $4.50/node/mo Low Zabbix Agent + SNMP + discovery Interval / triggers Community $0; support/cloud separate High New Relic Agent → ingest Interval Hosts unlimited; GB + seats ($0.40/GB after 100 GB free) Low (SaaS) Checkmk Agent + SNMP + discovery Interval Community about 100 hosts; Pro from €190/mo Medium–high  How we scored: collection model (agent vs scrape vs SNMP), metric resolution, invoice growth at fixed host count, and who keeps the monitoring plane alive. License-free is not free if a platform engineer is unavailable for HA and retention. Get posts like this in your inbox Engineering insights on monitoring, incidents, and uptime. Bi-weekly, 2-minute read. Join free Datadog  Datadog is the commercial default for "agent on every host." Infrastructure Pro is $15/host/month annual ($18 on-demand), 15-month retention, 1,000+ integrations. Free: 5 hosts, 1-day retention.  The agent covers host metrics, containers, and a large integration catalog for databases and queues. Live Processes and ML alerts sit on Enterprise ($23/host/mo annual). APM, logs, custom metrics, and synthetics are separate meters. That design wins RFPs and surprises mid-size fleets once every product line is enabled. Container billing (free allotment per host, then per-container charges) is the usual Kubernetes surprise.  Pick it when you want one vendor from host metrics into APM and can forecast stacked meters. Skip it when you only need CPU/disk and will not buy the rest of the suite.  Prometheus + Grafana  Prometheus scrapes exporters (node_exporter on hosts, kube-state-metrics and cAdvisor in clusters). You query with PromQL and route with Alertmanager. Grafana is the dashboard layer most operators already know. There is no license fee.  The real cost is operating the TSDB, protecting scrape targets from cardinality explosions, and eventually adding Thanos, Mimir, or VictoriaMetrics when a single Prometheus instance is not enough. Hiring is easy because the stack is an industry default. Owning upgrades, HA, and "who watches the watcher" is not optional.  Pick it when you run Kubernetes and Platform owns Helm charts. Skip it when a five-person product team would be unpaid Prometheus ops.  Grafana Cloud  Grafana Cloud is managed Prometheus-compatible metrics (plus Loki logs and Tempo traces). Free: 10k active series, 14-day retention. Pro: $19/mo platform fee, longer metric retention, then series billing (list from $6.50 per 1k series, with volume discounts).  Ship metrics with Grafana Agent or Alloy, keep PromQL, skip running Mimir yourself. The failure mode is identical to self-hosted Prometheus: a careless label set multiplies active series overnight. Treat series count as a first-class SLO, not a vague "usage" line.  Pick it when you want PromQL without running storage backends. Skip it when you need SNMP-first discovery for mixed physical estates (look at Zabbix or Checkmk instead).  Netdata  Netdata is per-second, auto-discovered host charts with almost no config. Install the agent, open the local UI or connect nodes to Cloud, and you get thousands of charts for CPU, disks, network, containers, and apps the agent can detect.  Community Cloud: 5 connected nodes free. Business: $4.50/node/month (annual), with metrics staying on-prem and Cloud used for access and aggregation. That model fits teams that refuse to ship every sample to a third-party TSDB.  Pick it when you need "what is this box doing right now?" in minutes. Skip it when the job is multi-year PromQL capacity across clusters, or mixed SNMP gear that Zabbix/Checkmk already understand.  Zabbix  Zabbix is the classic agent + SNMP + discovery stack for physical hosts, VMs, switches, and apps that never learned exporters. Community is free to self-host; paid support, training, and Zabbix Cloud attach a vendor when you need one.  Templates and auto-discovery cut per-host toil once the framework exists. The cost is learning curve and a permanently owned Zabbix server. The UI and template model feel heavy if your entire world is Kubernetes with a funded PromQL shop.  Pick it when exporters are not realistic and remote or multi-site discovery still matters. Skip it when you have already standardized on exporters and Helm.  New Relic  New Relic meters data ingest and seats, not hosts. Free: 100 GB/mo and one full platform user across infrastructure, APM, logs, and synthetics. Then $0.40/GB on the original data option. Full-platform seats climb quickly on Standard and Pro (Pro full users list around $349/user/mo annual).  The pitch for server fleets is simple: instrument many hosts without a $15×N Infrastructure line item. The failure mode is ingest growth from verbose logs and high-cardinality custom metrics, plus seat sprawl when every engineer needs the full UI.  Pick it when unlimited hosts under an ingest bill is clearer for finance than Datadog's per-host model. Skip it when you only need host metrics and will not use the rest of the platform.  Checkmk  Checkmk auto-discovers hosts and services (disk mounts, interfaces, application checks; roughly 30 services per host in their sizing guidance). Community covers smaller estates. Pro starts around €190/mo billed annually (about €1.90/host at the 100-host reference). Ultimate and Cloud editions widen the observability surface.  Compared with assembling Prometheus exporters for every legacy box, Checkmk's discovery story is often faster for racked servers and Windows fleets. Community is intentionally capped; paid editions are IT-ops products, not developer-first monitoring-as-code for SaaS apps.  Pick it when heterogeneous hosts and SNMP devices are the daily job. Skip it when you want zero self-host ops and a pure SaaS agent.  Alternatives and head-to-heads  If you already run one tool, start here instead of re-reading every profile above.  Intent Prefer Avoid thinking Datadog alternative (host metrics only) Netdata, Prometheus+Grafana, Grafana Cloud, or New Relic That any of these replaces Datadog APM + logs by itself Open-source Datadog alternative Prometheus stack; Netdata for speed; Zabbix/Checkmk for SNMP "Free" with no platform owner Datadog vs Prometheus Prom: license + K8s gravity. Datadog: time-to-value + support Prometheus as free Datadog with zero ops Datadog vs Grafana Cloud Grafana Cloud if you speak PromQL; Datadog for turnkey agent → APM Either as an SNMP-first estate tool Datadog vs New Relic New Relic: hosts unlimited, pay GB/seats. Datadog: clearer per-host forecasting Ignoring log/cardinality growth on both Prometheus vs Grafana Use together (store vs visualize), or Grafana Cloud for both managed Buying them as competing host agents Netdata vs Prometheus Netdata: per-second triage. Prometheus: long retention + federation Replacing a mature Prom install with Netdata for planning alone Zabbix vs Prometheus Zabbix: physical/SNMP. Prometheus: exporters/K8s One tool forced to own both without exporters and SNMP Checkmk vs Zabbix Same job family. Checkmk: paid efficiency + service pricing. Zabbix: Community + templates Treating either as an uptime-ping SaaS  Full-suite comparisons beyond host agents: Datadog vs Dynatrace .  How to choose   Need SNMP and auto-discovery on mixed physical gear → Zabbix or Checkmk .  Need Kubernetes exporters and can operate a TSDB → Prometheus + Grafana (or Grafana Cloud if you cannot).  Need per-second triage on a few hosts today → Netdata .  Need commercial host agent with a path into APM → Datadog or New Relic (pick the meter your finance team can forecast).  Host layer is green; users still break on vendors/APIs → add external checks .   A sane default stack: Netdata or Prometheus for host truth, plus an outside-in layer for customer paths. One megasuite for everything works only when budget and org chart match.  FAQ  What should I use for server host metrics in 2026?  Datadog for commercial default. Prometheus + Grafana or Netdata for open source. Zabbix or Checkmk for SNMP estates. New Relic or Grafana Cloud when you want managed SaaS without Datadog's host meter.  Datadog alternative for servers only?  Netdata or Prometheus for metrics. New Relic or Grafana Cloud for managed billing without per-host Infrastructure Pro. None of those is a one-click Datadog suite replacement.  Prometheus or Datadog?  Prometheus if Platform owns scrapes and storage. Datadog if engineering time is scarcer than license cost and you may buy APM next.  Host performance vs uptime monitoring?  Host tools watch the machine. Uptime tools watch whether users can reach the service. Most teams need both; they are different invoices.  Related guides   Datadog vs Dynatrace  Best cloud monitoring tools  Best open-source monitoring tools  Best website monitoring tools  Best API monitoring tools   Next step  Choose the host collector first. When that layer is green and users still fail, add external checks ( DevHelm free tier if you want flat pricing and a status page without another per-host meter). DevHelm .io Product Uptime Monitoring HTTP, TCP, DNS, ICMP, MCP checks from 4 global regions with 30s intervals Browser Testing Beta Run Playwright checks for your critical browser journeys Dependency Intelligence Track 80+ external services, automatic correlation with your monitors Status Pages Branded, real-time status pages on your domain — included from the free tier Pricing Blog Docs Log in Start Free Start Free Blog Guides Infrastructure Playwright What Is Playwright? A Practical Guide for Developers DevHelm Team / Jul 10, 2026 / 19 min read Playwright is Microsoft's open-source browser automation tool. It drives Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit through one API, runs headless in CI, and is the default choice for Playwright testing in 2026. If you need to click buttons, fill forms, and assert on what users actually see, this is the library most teams reach for first.  This guide answers what Playwright is, what it does, how Playwright testing differs from Playwright automation, and how to use Playwright with Python from a minimal script through a real login and GitHub Actions. For the official API reference and language guides, see playwright.dev . Working Python demos for every step below live in the companion repo: github.com/Inekss/test_playwright .  What is Playwright  Playwright is a browser automation tool you install and run yourself. It is not a cloud product and not a full product suite. Bindings exist for JavaScript/TypeScript, Python, Java, and .NET.  What does Playwright do  You use it to:   Launch a browser (headless or headed).  Open pages and navigate URLs.  Interact: click a button, type, upload files, intercept network.  Assert on DOM state, accessibility trees, responses, and console output.  Capture a Playwright screenshot or a trace when something fails.   The object model has four layers:  Layer Role Typical call Browser Engine process chromium.launch() BrowserContext Isolated session (cookies, storage) browser.new_context() Page One tab context.new_page() Locator Element handle with auto-waiting page.get_by_role("button", name="Sign in")  The design bet is web-first assertions. Instead of sleep(3) and hoping the DOM updated, you wait on a condition: the element is visible, the text matches, the URL changed. Playwright retries until the condition holds or a timeout expires. That auto-waiting is why the same scripts stay stable in CI and when you later schedule them against production as continuous checks. Running those journeys without a visible window is covered under headless browser checks; headless browser monitoring .  Is Playwright open source  Yes. Playwright is Apache 2.0, maintained by Microsoft. You install the language package, then download browser binaries with playwright install . There is no license fee for the tool itself.  Minimal script (Python)  from playwright . sync_api import sync_playwright  with sync_playwright ( )  as p :  browser = p . chromium . launch ( headless = True )  page = browser . new_page ( )  page . goto ( "https://playwright.dev/python/" )   print ( page . title ( ) )  # "Playwright Python"  browser . close ( )  Same idea in TypeScript  import  { chromium }  from  "playwright" ;   const browser =  await chromium . launch ( { headless :  true  } ) ;  const page =  await browser . newPage ( ) ;  await page . goto ( "https://playwright.dev/" ) ;  console . log ( await page . title ( ) ) ;  await browser . close ( ) ;  Same model in both languages: launch → new page → goto → assert or read. This page is the practical overview; use the official docs linked above for the full API reference by language.  What is a Page in Playwright  A Page is one browser tab. Almost every action in Playwright testing goes through it: navigate, find elements, click, type, read the title, take a screenshot.  Navigate and inspect  page . goto ( "https://playwright.dev/python/" )  print ( page . title ( ) )  print ( page . url )  page . reload ( )  page . go_back ( )  goto waits for the load state you ask for (default load ). Prefer asserting on content over wait_for_load_state("networkidle") when the page keeps open connections.  Find elements (prefer these over raw CSS)  page . get_by_role ( "button" , name = "Get started" )  page . get_by_label ( "Email address" )  page . get_by_placeholder ( "Search" )  page . get_by_text ( "Docs" )  page . get_by_test_id ( "submit" )  page . locator ( "css=.legacy-only-when-needed" )  Role and label locators match how assistive tech sees the page. They survive CSS refactors better than .btn-primary-2 .  Playwright click (and fill)  To click a button or link, prefer role-based locators:  page . get_by_role ( "link" , name = "Docs" ) . click ( )  page . get_by_role ( "button" , name = "Continue" , exact = True ) . click ( )  page . get_by_label ( "Email address" ) . fill ( "user@example.com" )  # Prefer role=textbox for password fields (see login example below)  page . get_by_role ( "textbox" , name = "Password" ) . fill ( "secret" )  page . locator ( "input[type=file]" ) . set_input_files ( "receipt.pdf" )  fill clears the field and types the value. click auto-waits until the control is visible, enabled, and stable. That built-in wait is why you rarely need a fixed sleep before a Playwright click.  Playwright wait, expect, and assertions  Playwright wait behavior is built into actions and into expect . Assertions in Playwright are web-first: they retry until the condition holds or the timeout expires.  from playwright . sync_api import expect  page . wait_for_url ( "**/dashboard" )  expect ( page . get_by_role ( "heading" , name = "Dashboard" ) ) . to_be_visible ( )  expect ( page ) . to_have_title ( "Dashboard" )  expect ( page . get_by_text ( "Welcome back" ) ) . to_contain_text ( "Welcome" )  Common Playwright expect checks: to_be_visible , to_have_title , to_have_url , to_contain_text , to_have_count . Prefer these Playwright assertions over assert element.is_visible() after a manual sleep.  Playwright screenshot and traces  page . screenshot ( path = "failure.png" , full_page = True )   # Trace for CI / monitoring forensics  context = browser . new_context ( )  context . tracing . start ( screenshots = True , snapshots = True , sources = True )  page = context . new_page ( )  # ... run the journey ...  context . tracing . stop ( path = "trace.zip" )  # Open with: playwright show-trace trace.zip  A Locator is not a snapshot of the DOM at query time. It re-resolves when you act on it. Playwright auto-waits for the element to be actionable before each action. When a scheduled check fails, screenshot plus trace is how you debug without reproducing by hand. For a deeper look at failure forensics in browser checks, browser monitoring with Playwright .  Playwright codegen  To record a flow instead of writing locators by hand:  playwright codegen https://app.devhelm.io/login  Copy the generated locators into a small class, then tighten them (exact button names, role=textbox for password). Codegen is the fastest way to draft a first script; production checks still need stable roles and assertions. Get posts like this in your inbox Engineering insights on monitoring, incidents, and uptime. Bi-weekly, 2-minute read. Join free What is Playwright testing vs Playwright automation  The same Playwright automation tool shows up under two search intents:   Playwright testing usually means end-to-end checks in a test runner (pytest, Jest, or @playwright/test ). Goal: catch regressions before merge.  Playwright automation is the broader capability: drive a browser for scraping, codegen, PDF generation, screenshots, or scheduled health checks. Goal: make the browser do work without a human.   Same API. Different cadence and environment. A checkout flow you assert in CI is Playwright testing. That same flow run every 15 minutes against production is still automation, now aimed at reliability. For how to schedule an existing journey as a continuous check, Playwright monitoring .  Why Playwright matters for monitoring  CI answers "did this branch break the app?" It does not answer "is production working for users right now?" A third-party script, a CDN blip, or a half-failed deploy can break a journey after merge, when nothing re-runs the suite.  Running browser scripts on a schedule against live URLs closes that gap. That practice is synthetic monitoring: outside-in checks that assert what users see, not only what the server returns. what synthetic monitoring is . Teams already writing Playwright tests get a short path: reuse the journey, schedule it, alert on failure. The Node scheduling and failure-forensics paths are covered in the linked guides above. Below is how to use Playwright with Python.  How to use Playwright with Python  Most tutorials assume TypeScript. Python teams (Django, FastAPI, data platforms) often want the same browser automation in the language they already ship.  Playwright Python has two APIs:   Sync ( playwright.sync_api ): blocking calls, reads like a script. Best for cron jobs, one-off checks, and learning.  Async ( playwright.async_api ): async/await , for asyncio services.   For learning and scheduled checks, sync is enough. Prefer role- and label-based locators over brittle CSS.  Clone the example repo and follow along: github.com/Inekss/test_playwright . It has runnable code for every step below. Four practical topics on this page:   Simple setup with Playwright : install Playwright and prove the browser works.  Example of usage with Playwright : open a real site, locate elements, count them.  Simulate login with Playwright : email + password on app.devhelm.io with your own account.  Automation with GitHub Actions : run the blog-count check in GitHub Actions.   Project layout  Path Role main.py Config constants + if __name__ == "__main__" run_ci.py CI entrypoint: blog count only (no login) .github/workflows/blog-count.yml Runs run_ci.py on push/PR to main utils/browser.py BrowserSession (open/close Chromium) checks/smoke.py Setup check: goto URL, assert title checks/blog_count.py Usage example: count post cards on a listing page examples/login/login_check.py Login example: Auth0 email/password on app.devhelm.io  Shared browser session  Reuse one Chromium process across checks:  # utils/browser.py  from typing import Optional  from playwright . sync_api import Browser , Page , Playwright , sync_playwright   class  BrowserSession :   """Open one Chromium tab, close it when done."""    def  __init__ ( self , headless :  bool  =  True )  - >  None :  self . headless = headless self . _playwright : Optional [ Playwright ]  =  None  self . _browser : Optional [ Browser ]  =  None  self . page : Optional [ Page ]  =  None    def  __enter__ ( self )  - >  "BrowserSession" :  self . _playwright = sync_playwright ( ) . start ( )  self . _browser = self . _playwright . chromium . launch ( headless = self . headless )  self . page = self . _browser . new_page ( )   return self   def  __exit__ ( self ,  * _exc :  object )  - >  None :   if self . _browser is  not  None :  self . _browser . close ( )   if self . _playwright is  not  None :  self . _playwright . stop ( )  Set headless=False while debugging so you can watch the browser.  1. Simple setup with Playwright  Goal: confirm pip , the playwright package, and Chromium are installed. No product logic yet, only "can I launch a browser and read a title?"  Install once:  python -m venv .venv # Windows:  .venv\Scripts\activate  # macOS/Linux: source .venv/bin/activate   pip install  -r requirements.txt # playwright>=1.44  playwright install chromium  The setup check:  # checks/smoke.py  from playwright . sync_api import Page   class  SmokeCheck :   def  __init__ ( self , url :  str , expected_title :  str )  - >  None :  self . url = url self . expected_title = expected_title   def  run ( self , page : Page )  - >  str :  page . goto ( self . url )  title = page . title ( )   assert title == self . expected_title ,  f"Unexpected title: { title !r } "   return title  Wire it in main.py :  SMOKE_URL =  "https://playwright.dev/python/"  SMOKE_EXPECTED_TITLE =  "Playwright Python"   with BrowserSession ( headless = True )  as session :   assert session . page is  not  None  title = SmokeCheck ( SMOKE_URL , SMOKE_EXPECTED_TITLE ) . run ( session . page )   print ( f"OK: { title } " )  Run:  python main.py  You are set up when the output includes:  OK: Playwright Python  If that line is missing or the assert fails, fix install before anything else: re-run pip install -r requirements.txt and playwright install chromium . Page titles on third-party sites do change; if the assert fails with a different string, print page.title() and update the constant.  2. Example of usage with Playwright  Goal: use the same Page API on a live site. Open https://devhelm.io/blog , find article cards, and print how many are on the page. Today that listing shows 20 posts, so the script prints:  Blog posts on page: 20  Each card is a link to /blog/<slug> with an h2 title:  # checks/blog_count.py  from playwright . sync_api import Page   class  BlogCountCheck :   def  __init__ ( self , url :  str )  - >  None :  self . url = url   def  run ( self , page : Page )  - >  int :  page . goto ( self . url )  cards = page . locator ( 'a[href^="/blog/"] h2' )  cards . first . wait_for ( state = "visible" )   return cards . count ( )  BLOG_URL =  "https://devhelm.io/blog"   count = BlogCountCheck ( BLOG_URL ) . run ( session . page )  print ( f"Blog posts on page: { count } " )  What this example shows:   page.goto : navigate  page.locator : find elements  wait_for : wait for the page to be ready (no sleep )  count : read a number from the DOM   You can also assert with expect instead of returning a count:  from playwright . sync_api import expect  page . goto ( "https://devhelm.io/blog" )  cards = page . locator ( 'a[href^="/blog/"] h2' )  expect ( cards . first ) . to_be_visible ( )  expect ( cards ) . not_to_have_count ( 0 )  Counting cards on a public listing is a light example of scraping-style automation: open the page, wait for the list, read the DOM. The same pattern scales to checkout pages, search results, and pricing tables once you swap the locator.  3. Simulate login with Playwright  Goal: drive a real multi-step login. https://app.devhelm.io/login redirects to Auth0: email → Continue → password → Continue → back to the app.  Use your own DevHelm account. Put the values in main.py (leave them empty so the public repo skips this step):  LOGIN_URL =  "https://app.devhelm.io/login"  LOGIN_EMAIL =  ""  # set your own  LOGIN_PASSWORD =  ""  # set your own  The check:  # examples/login/login_check.py  import re  from playwright . sync_api import Page , expect   class  LoginCheck :   """Two-step Auth0 login: email → Continue → password → Continue."""    def  __init__ ( self , url :  str , email :  str , password :  str )  - >  None :  self . url = url self . email = email self . password = password   def  run ( self , page : Page )  - >  str :  page . goto ( self . url )   page . get_by_label ( "Email address" ) . fill ( self . email )  page . get_by_role ( "button" , name = "Continue" , exact = True ) . click ( )    # Auth0 also renders a "Show password" switch whose aria-label   # matches get_by_label("Password") and trips strict mode.  password = page . get_by_role ( "textbox" , name = "Password" )  password . wait_for ( state = "visible" )  password . fill ( self . password )  page . get_by_role ( "button" , name = "Continue" , exact = True ) . click ( )   expect ( page ) . to_have_url (  re . compile ( r"https://app\.devhelm\.io/" ) ,  timeout = 30_000 ,   )   assert  "/u/login"  not  in page . url ,  f"Still on Auth0: { page . url } "   return page . url  Wire it:  if LOGIN_EMAIL and LOGIN_PASSWORD :  url = LoginCheck ( LOGIN_URL , LOGIN_EMAIL , LOGIN_PASSWORD ) . run ( session . page )   print ( f"Logged in: { url } " )  else :   print ( "Skip login: set LOGIN_EMAIL and LOGIN_PASSWORD in main.py" )  What this example shows:   Multi-step forms (email screen, then password screen)  Role/label locators on a real Auth0 UI  Strict-mode pitfalls when two controls share a label substring  Waiting for a post-login URL instead of a fixed sleep   Do not commit real passwords. Keep credentials only in your local main.py . Login is the journey most teams promote from a local script into a scheduled production check first, because auth breaks silently and status codes alone miss it.  4. Automation with GitHub Actions  A script that only runs on your laptop is not automation yet. Step 4 lives in github.com/Inekss/test_playwright , not in a monorepo. On every push or merge to main , GitHub Actions runs the blog-count check against https://devhelm.io/blog . No login, no secrets. Keeping checks in git so environments stay reproducible is the same idea as monitoring as code; monitoring as code .  CI entrypoint ( run_ci.py ):  # run_ci.py  from checks . blog_count import BlogCountCheck from utils . browser import BrowserSession  BLOG_URL =  "https://devhelm.io/blog"  EXPECTED_MIN_POSTS =  20    def  main ( )  - >  None :   with BrowserSession ( headless = True )  as session :   assert session . page is  not  None  count = BlogCountCheck ( BLOG_URL ) . run ( session . page )    print ( f"Blog posts on page: { count } " )   assert count >= EXPECTED_MIN_POSTS ,  f"expected >= { EXPECTED_MIN_POSTS } , got { count } "   print ( f"OK: { count } >= { EXPECTED_MIN_POSTS } " )    if __name__ ==  "__main__" :  main ( )  Workflow ( .github/workflows/blog-count.yml in the test_playwright repo):  name : Blog count  on :   push :   branches :  [ main ]   pull_request :   branches :  [ main ]   workflow_dispatch :   jobs :   blog-count :   name : Count posts on devhelm.io/blog  runs-on : ubuntu - latest  timeout-minutes :  10    steps :   -  uses : actions/checkout@v4   -  name : Set up Python  uses : actions/setup - python@v5  with :   python-version :  "3.12"    -  name : Install dependencies  run :  |  pip install -r requirements.txt playwright install --with-deps chromium    -  name : Count blog posts  run : python run_ci.py  env :   BLOG_URL : https : //devhelm.io/blog  EXPECTED_MIN_POSTS :  "20"  What this step shows:   Same BlogCountCheck as step 2, now headless in CI  Runs on every push to main and on every PR into main (merge path)  Repo root is the project: no working-directory prefix  A floor of 20 posts ( EXPECTED_MIN_POSTS ) so the check stays green as the listing grows  No credentials in the workflow   Locally mirror CI with python run_ci.py . On failure the job exits non-zero and the PR (or push to main ) stays red until the listing or the locator is fixed.  Full main.py entrypoint  from checks . blog_count import BlogCountCheck from checks . smoke import SmokeCheck from examples . login . login_check import LoginCheck from utils . browser import BrowserSession  HEADLESS =  True  SMOKE_URL =  "https://playwright.dev/python/"  SMOKE_EXPECTED_TITLE =  "Playwright Python"  BLOG_URL =  "https://devhelm.io/blog"  LOGIN_URL =  "https://app.devhelm.io/login"  LOGIN_EMAIL =  ""  LOGIN_PASSWORD =  ""    def  main ( )  - >  None :   with BrowserSession ( headless = HEADLESS )  as session :   assert session . page is  not  None   title = SmokeCheck ( SMOKE_URL , SMOKE_EXPECTED_TITLE ) . run ( session . page )   print ( f"OK: { title } " )   count = BlogCountCheck ( BLOG_URL ) . run ( session . page )   print ( f"Blog posts on page: { count } " )    if LOGIN_EMAIL and LOGIN_PASSWORD :  url = LoginCheck ( LOGIN_URL , LOGIN_EMAIL , LOGIN_PASSWORD ) . run (  session . page  )   print ( f"Logged in: { url } " )   else :   print ( "Skip login: set LOGIN_EMAIL and LOGIN_PASSWORD in main.py" )    if __name__ ==  "__main__" :  main ( )  Example output (with login configured):  OK: Playwright Python
Blog posts on page: 20
Logged in: https://app.devhelm.io/...  Common pitfalls (with fixes)  Strict mode violation.  get_by_label("Password") can match both the password input and a "Show password" toggle. Prefer get_by_role("textbox", name="Password") or page.locator("#password") .  # Bad: may match 2 elements  page . get_by_label ( "Password" ) . fill ( secret )   # Good: one input  page . get_by_role ( "textbox" , name = "Password" ) . fill ( secret )  Fixed sleeps. Prefer expect / wait_for over time.sleep(3) . Sleeps flake under load and slow CI.  # Bad  time . sleep ( 3 )  assert page . get_by_text ( "Done" ) . is_visible ( )   # Good  expect ( page . get_by_text ( "Done" ) ) . to_be_visible ( )  Brittle CSS. Prefer roles, labels, and data-testid over hashed class names.  # Bad: breaks on redesign  page . locator ( ".css-1a2b3c > button" ) . click ( )   # Good  page . get_by_role ( "button" , name = "Save" ) . click ( )  # or  page . get_by_test_id ( "save-button" ) . click ( )  Headed debug. When a headless run fails, re-run with headless=False and optionally slow the actions:  browser = p . chromium . launch ( headless = False , slow_mo = 200 )  Codegen. To record a flow instead of writing locators by hand, use playwright codegen (see the Playwright codegen section above). Copy the generated locators into a class like LoginCheck , then tighten them (exact button names, role=textbox for password).  When a CI or scheduled run fails, fix the locator or the product, then make sure alerts fire only on real breakage. Noisy pages create alert fatigue; for how to keep monitoring signals actionable, alert fatigue .  From local script to production monitor  A script that passes on your laptop is a CI check or a monitor waiting for a schedule. The path is the same for most teams: write the journey locally, run it in CI on every PR, capture screenshot and trace on failure, then schedule it against production and alert when it fails.  The most common Playwright usage patterns teams automate this way:   Login — email/password or SSO, then assert the post-auth landing page  Checkout — add to cart, fill payment fields, confirm the order success screen  Form submit — signup, contact, or settings save with validation and redirect checks  Search and filter — type a query, wait for results, assert count or first hit  Scraping / data extraction — open listing pages, collect titles, prices, or links  File upload — attach a document, wait for processing, assert the confirmation state  Multi-step wizards — onboarding or checkout flows across several screens  Auth-gated dashboards — after login, assert charts, tables, or empty states load   Once the journey is stable locally and in CI, schedule the same script against production. That is the move from a local Playwright script to a production monitor. For how outside-in browser checks fit next to other synthetic practices, synthetic monitoring best practices . When you are choosing a platform rather than writing the runner yourself, best synthetic monitoring tools . title: Best Cloud Monitoring Tools in 2026: A Developer's Honest Comparison — DevHelm
text: DevHelm .io Product Uptime Monitoring HTTP, TCP, DNS, ICMP, MCP checks from 4 global regions with 30s intervals Browser Testing Beta Run Playwright checks for your critical browser journeys Dependency Intelligence Track 80+ external services, automatic correlation with your monitors Status Pages Branded, real-time status pages on your domain — included from the free tier Pricing Blog Docs Log in Start Free Start Free Blog Comparisons Guides Best Cloud Monitoring Tools in 2026: A Developer's Honest Comparison DevHelm Team / Jul 7, 2026 / 16 min read Your app runs across three AWS regions, a managed Postgres instance, a Stripe integration, and an OpenAI dependency. Something slows down at 2 AM. Is it your containers? A regional network blip? A vendor degradation you have no control over? "Cloud monitoring" is supposed to answer that question, but the category is so broad that two tools both claiming the label can solve completely different problems.  Some tools ingest host metrics, traces, and logs from your infrastructure (CPU, memory, container restarts, slow queries). Others watch your services from the outside: endpoints, SSL, response bodies. They correlate failures with the third-party clouds you depend on. Most teams need both layers, and the mistake is buying one when you needed the other.  We compared nine tools across the dimensions that actually decide the purchase: infrastructure metrics, APM and tracing, log management, external endpoint checks, multi-cloud coverage, and the one that surprises finance teams: how the bill scales. This comparison maps each tool to the job it actually does, whether you're on a single provider or spanning AWS, Azure, and GCP. Every pricing model below was checked against official pages in July 2026.  TL;DR comparison  Tool What it monitors Best For Model Free Tier Entry Price DevHelm API & web endpoints (HTTP), SSL, DNS, TCP, cron/heartbeats + third-party dependencies — external only, no host metrics or logs External + dependency monitoring for cloud-hosted apps Flat monthly 50 monitors, 5-min $12/mo Datadog Host/infra metrics, APM & traces, logs, synthetics, RUM, security Full-stack observability across infra, APM, and logs Usage + per-host Limited $15/host/mo Amazon CloudWatch AWS metrics, logs, alarms, synthetic canaries (AWS only) AWS-native metrics, logs, and alarms Pay-as-you-go Basic metrics free Usage-based Google Cloud Monitoring GCP metrics, uptime checks, logs, traces (GCP only) GCP-native observability (Cloud Operations) Pay-as-you-go Generous allotment Usage-based Azure Monitor Azure metrics, logs (Log Analytics), APM (App Insights) — Azure only Azure-native metrics and Log Analytics Pay-as-you-go Basic metrics free Usage-based New Relic Infra metrics, APM & traces, logs, synthetics, RUM All-in-one observability with data-based pricing Data + per-user 100 GB/mo, 1 user $0.35/GB Dynatrace Infra metrics, APM & traces, logs, synthetics — full-stack Enterprise AI-driven full-stack monitoring Consumption (DPS) 15-day trial ~$0.08/host-hr Grafana Cloud Metrics (Prometheus), logs (Loki), traces (Tempo), synthetics Open-source stack (Prometheus, Loki, Tempo) managed Usage-based 10k series, 50 GB logs Usage-based Better Stack Uptime/endpoint checks, log management, on-call scheduling Uptime + logs + on-call in one dashboard Per-seat + usage 10 monitors, 3-min $29/mo/seat  How we evaluated  "Cloud monitoring" spans two problem domains that rarely live in the same product tier, so we scored each tool on both. Infrastructure telemetry : can it ingest metrics, traces, and logs from cloud hosts, containers, and managed services? External and dependency monitoring : can it check your endpoints from outside your cloud, validate responses, and tell you when a vendor (AWS, Stripe, a payments API) is the actual culprit? We also weighted multi-cloud coverage (does it work equally across AWS, Azure, and GCP, or is it locked to one provider?), alerting and correlation (how fast, and does it group related failures into one incident?), and pricing predictability (flat, per-host, per-GB, per-user, or consumption units, and what happens at scale). A tool that nails infra metrics but can't tell you a third-party API degraded is only doing half the job. Get posts like this in your inbox Engineering insights on monitoring, incidents, and uptime. It is not a CloudWatch replacement for host metrics. It is the black-box layer that answers "is my service actually working for users, and if not, is a vendor the reason?" Every monitor, including the free tier, supports HTTP checks with custom headers, request bodies, response body assertions, and SSL certificate monitoring.  The differentiator for cloud teams is resource groups. When Stripe degrades, your checkout monitor, billing webhook monitor, and subscription monitor would normally all fire separate alerts. Group them by the shared dependency and you get one alert that says "checkout is degraded, and the common factor is Stripe." Not seven pages at 2 AM. This is the alert-correlation problem that pure infra-metrics tools leave to you.  Because checks are defined through a CLI, Terraform provider, and SDKs (monitoring as code), your configuration lives in version control next to the infrastructure it watches:  # Monitor a cloud-hosted endpoint and a vendor cloud it depends on  devhelm monitor create --type http --url https://api.yourapp.com/health --interval 30s devhelm monitor create --type http --url https://api.stripe.com/healthcheck --assert-status 200  Key strengths   Response body assertions, custom headers, and request bodies on every plan including Free  Resource groups that correlate failures to a shared cloud dependency (one alert, not seven)  Cloud-agnostic: monitors services on AWS, Azure, GCP, or anywhere with a URL  CLI + Terraform + SDK for monitors defined as code, deployed in CI/CD  Flat pricing with no per-host, per-GB, or per-seat multipliers  30-second checks and a status page that auto-updates from monitor state   Pricing  Tier Price Monitors Check Interval Key Features Free $0/mo 50 5 min Response assertions, SSL monitoring, 1 status page Starter $12/mo 75 1 min All Free features + faster checks Pro $29/mo 250 30 sec All regions, resource groups, PagerDuty/Opsgenie Team $79/mo 500 30 sec SMS alerts, team management Business $249/mo 2,000 30 sec Unlimited team, white-label status pages  Cost traps   Resource groups and 30-second intervals require Pro ($29/mo)  SMS alerting is Team ($79/mo) and above   Limitations   No host metrics, container/Kubernetes telemetry, or APM. This is external and dependency monitoring, not infrastructure observability  No log ingestion or analytics. Pair it with a metrics/logs platform for full-stack coverage  Smaller global probe network than the hyperscalers (currently 6+ regions, expanding)   Best for: Teams running apps in the cloud who want fast external checks, response validation, and vendor-dependency correlation at flat pricing, layered on top of (or instead of) heavyweight infra tools.  Datadog  Datadog is the default answer when someone says "cloud monitoring platform." It covers infrastructure metrics, APM and distributed tracing, log management, synthetic checks, real user monitoring, and security across AWS, Azure, and GCP with 800+ integrations. If you want one pane of glass for everything your cloud does, Datadog is the most complete option on this list.  That completeness is also the catch. Datadog's pricing is a stack of independent products, each metered differently: infrastructure per host, APM per host, logs per GB ingested and retained, synthetics per run, custom metrics per series. A mid-size cloud footprint routinely produces a five-figure monthly bill. The line items that grow fastest (custom metrics and log retention) are the hardest to predict in advance.  Key strengths   Full-stack observability: infra, APM, logs, synthetics, RUM, security in one platform  800+ integrations covering every major cloud service and managed database  Strong multi-cloud support with no provider lock-in  Mature alerting with anomaly detection, forecasting, and composite monitors  Terraform provider and API for config-as-code   Pricing  Component Annual Price Notes Infrastructure $15/host/mo Entry point; per-host APM $31/host/mo On top of infra Log management $0.10/GB ingest + retention Retention billed separately Synthetic API tests $5/10k runs Location multiplier applies Custom metrics Usage-based Grows silently with cardinality  Cost traps   Every product is metered separately. The "starting at $15/host" number is rarely the real bill  Custom metrics billing scales with tag cardinality and surprises teams at renewal  Log retention is priced on top of ingestion, so long retention windows multiply cost  On-demand rates run well above annual-commit pricing   Limitations   Cost complexity makes budgeting genuinely hard at scale  Overkill for teams that only need external checks and uptime  Setup and tuning is a project, not an afternoon   Best for: Well-resourced teams that want one platform for infrastructure, APM, and logs across multiple clouds and can manage the billing complexity.  Amazon CloudWatch  Amazon CloudWatch is the native monitoring service for AWS. If your workloads run on EC2, Lambda, ECS, EKS, RDS, or virtually any AWS service, CloudWatch collects their metrics and logs with zero integration work. The data is already there. Alarms, dashboards, Logs Insights queries, and Synthetics canaries all live inside the AWS console and IAM model you already use.  The strength is also the boundary: CloudWatch is AWS-first. It can ingest custom metrics from anywhere, but its reason to exist is deep AWS coverage. Monitoring Azure or GCP through it is not the intended path. For an AWS-only shop, it's the lowest-friction option. For multi-cloud, it becomes one silo among several.  Key strengths   Native, zero-setup metrics and logs for AWS services  Alarms, dashboards, and Logs Insights built into the AWS console  CloudWatch Synthetics canaries for endpoint checks  Pay-as-you-go with a usable free tier for basic metrics  Deep integration with IAM, EventBridge, and Auto Scaling   Pricing  Component Price Notes Basic metrics Free Standard AWS service metrics Custom / detailed metrics ~$0.30/metric/mo First 10k, then tiered down Dashboards $3/dashboard/mo Beyond the free 3 Logs ingestion ~$0.50/GB Plus storage and Insights query cost Synthetics canaries ~$0.0012/run Per canary run  Cost traps   Custom metrics and high-resolution metrics add up quickly across many resources  Logs cost is ingestion + storage + query (three separate meters)  Cross-account and cross-region dashboards add operational and cost overhead   Limitations   AWS-centric, poor fit as a multi-cloud pane of glass  No APM in CloudWatch itself (that's AWS X-Ray, a separate service)  Alerting UX and correlation are basic compared to dedicated platforms   Best for: AWS-only teams that want native, low-friction infrastructure metrics, logs, and alarms without adding a third-party vendor.  Google Cloud Monitoring  Google Cloud Monitoring (part of the Cloud Operations suite, formerly Stackdriver) is GCP's native observability layer. It collects metrics, logs (via Cloud Logging), and traces (via Cloud Trace) from GKE, Compute Engine, Cloud Run, and the rest of Google Cloud, with uptime checks for external endpoints and SLO monitoring built in.  Its uptime-check and SLO tooling is genuinely good. You can define service-level objectives, track error budgets, and alert on burn rate without bolting on another tool. As with the other hyperscaler tools, the trade-off is gravity: it's built to monitor Google Cloud, and using it as your primary monitor for workloads on other clouds fights the grain.  Key strengths   Native metrics, logs, and traces across GCP services  Built-in uptime checks and SLO / error-budget monitoring  Generous free allotment for GCP-generated telemetry  Tight integration with GKE and Cloud Run  Terraform support for config-as-code   Pricing  Component Price Notes GCP metrics Free allotment Most Google Cloud metrics included Chargeable metrics ~$0.2580/MiB Beyond the free allotment Cloud Logging ~$0.50/GB First 50 GiB/project free Uptime checks Free tier Then usage-based  Cost traps   Chargeable custom metrics accrue by data volume, not count. High cardinality inflates it  Log ingestion beyond the free tier is billed per GB  Telemetry from non-GCP sources is billed as chargeable ingestion   Limitations   GCP-first, awkward as a multi-cloud primary  Alerting and dashboards are functional but less polished than Datadog or Dynatrace  Cross-project observability requires deliberate setup   Best for: GCP-centric teams that want native monitoring, logging, and SLO tracking without leaving Google Cloud.  Azure Monitor  Azure Monitor is Microsoft's native monitoring stack, combining platform metrics, Log Analytics (Kusto/KQL queries), and Application Insights for APM. For workloads on Azure VMs, AKS, App Service, and Functions, it collects telemetry natively and feeds a shared alerting and dashboarding layer.  Application Insights is the standout piece. It delivers real APM, distributed tracing, and availability tests for apps instrumented with its SDK. The cost center to watch is Log Analytics: nearly everything interesting flows through it, and it's billed per GB ingested, so verbose logging or broad diagnostic settings can drive the bill up faster than teams expect.  Key strengths   Native metrics, logs, and APM (Application Insights) for Azure workloads  Powerful KQL querying in Log Analytics  Availability tests for external endpoint monitoring  Deep integration with Azure RBAC, resource groups, and Bicep/ARM  Terraform support for config-as-code   Pricing  Component Price Notes Platform metrics Free Standard Azure resource metrics Log Analytics ingestion ~$2.30/GB The primary cost driver Application Insights Billed via Log Analytics Ingestion-based Alert rules Per rule/mo Metric and log alerts priced separately  Cost traps   Log Analytics ingestion is the silent budget-killer. Diagnostic settings can flood it  Data retention beyond the included period is billed separately  Alert rules and notifications carry their own per-rule charges   Limitations   Azure-first, not a natural multi-cloud primary  Log Analytics has a learning curve (KQL) for teams new to it  Cost governance requires active management of ingestion settings   Best for: Azure-centric teams that want native infrastructure metrics, APM via Application Insights, and KQL-powered log analytics.  New Relic  New Relic rebuilt its pricing around data rather than hosts: you pay for gigabytes of telemetry ingested and for the number of full-platform users, not per monitored host. That change made it one of the more approachable all-in-one platforms for cloud monitoring. Infrastructure, APM, logs, synthetics, and browser monitoring under one meter, across all major clouds.  The free tier is unusually generous (100 GB of ingest per month and one full user), which makes New Relic viable for small teams doing real observability at zero cost. The two things to model carefully are data volume (high-cardinality custom events and verbose logs eat the GB allowance) and the per-full-user charge, which is where multi-engineer teams accrue cost.  Key strengths   Full-stack observability: infra, APM, logs, synthetics, browser, mobile  Data-based pricing decouples cost from host count  Genuinely useful free tier (100 GB/mo, 1 full user)  Strong multi-cloud coverage and 700+ integrations  Config-as-code via Terraform and API   Pricing  Component Price Notes Free tier $0 100 GB/mo ingest, 1 full user Data ingest $0.35/GB Beyond the free 100 GB Standard full user ~$99/user/mo Core (limited) users cheaper Data Plus $0.55/GB Higher-compliance ingest tier  Cost traps   Full-user seats are the main cost lever. Model your team size, not just data  High-cardinality custom metrics and events consume the GB allowance fast  Verbose application logs can blow past the free ingest tier quickly   Limitations   Data + user pricing takes effort to forecast accurately  Feature depth means a steeper onboarding than single-purpose tools  Some advanced capabilities gate behind higher-cost user tiers   Best for: Small-to-mid teams that want all-in-one observability with pricing that scales on data volume rather than host count.  Dynatrace  Dynatrace targets the enterprise end of cloud monitoring with a heavy bet on automation and AI. Its OneAgent auto-discovers services and dependencies, and the Davis AI engine does automated root-cause analysis. Instead of a wall of correlated alerts, it aims to tell you the single underlying cause of an incident. For large, complex, multi-cloud estates, that automation is the core value proposition.  Pricing moved to a consumption model (Dynatrace Platform Subscription) metered in granular units for full-stack monitoring, log ingestion, and synthetics. It's genuinely capable and genuinely expensive. Dynatrace is rarely the choice for a small team, and there's no free tier (evaluation is a 15-day trial).  Key strengths   OneAgent auto-instrumentation with minimal manual setup for discovery  Davis AI for automated root-cause analysis and anomaly detection  Full-stack: infra, APM, logs, synthetics, RUM across clouds  Strong Kubernetes and large-scale enterprise support  Config-as-code via Terraform and API   Pricing  Component Price Notes Full-stack monitoring ~$0.08/host-hour (8 GB) Consumption units (DPS) Log management ~$0.20/GB ingest + retention Metered separately Synthetic monitoring Per-request units Consumption-based Free tier None 15-day trial only  Cost traps   Consumption units make total cost hard to estimate before you're running at scale  Log ingestion and retention are separate meters on top of host monitoring  Enterprise contracts and minimums put it out of reach for small teams   Limitations   No free tier (trial only)  Enterprise pricing and complexity are overkill for straightforward cloud monitoring  Full value depends on adopting the OneAgent/Davis model end to end   Best for: Large enterprises with complex multi-cloud environments that want AI-driven root-cause analysis and can commit to consumption-based pricing.  Grafana Cloud  Grafana Cloud is the managed version of the open-source observability stack: Prometheus-compatible metrics (Mimir), Loki for logs, Tempo for traces, and Grafana dashboards on top. If your team already lives in Prometheus and Grafana, this is the path to keep that stack without running the storage backends yourself, and it works across any cloud that can ship metrics.  The model is usage-based across metrics series, log volume, and trace volume, with a real free tier (10k active series, 50 GB logs, 50 GB traces, three users). The trade-offs are the ones inherent to the open-source stack: you assemble and tune it yourself, and Prometheus cardinality management becomes your responsibility. Active series are the meter, and a careless label can multiply them.  Key strengths   Managed Prometheus, Loki, and Tempo with no backend ops  Cloud-agnostic: monitors anything that exposes Prometheus metrics  Genuinely useful free tier (10k series, 50 GB logs, 3 users)  Synthetic monitoring and OnCall available in the platform  Config-as-code via Terraform and Jsonnet; huge library of prebuilt dashboards   Pricing  Component Price Notes Free tier $0 10k series, 50 GB logs, 50 GB traces, 3 users Metrics Usage-based Per active series beyond free Logs / traces Usage-based Per GB ingested beyond free Pro / Advanced From ~$8/mo base + usage Scales with volume  Cost traps   Active-series cardinality is the meter. A bad label explodes both cost and load  Logs and traces are separate GB meters on top of metrics  Assembling and tuning the stack is engineering time, even when managed   Limitations   More assembly and tuning than turnkey platforms  APM is trace-based (Tempo), not a packaged APM product  Best value assumes existing Prometheus/Grafana familiarity   Best for: Teams already invested in Prometheus and Grafana who want a managed, cloud-agnostic stack without operating the storage layer.  Better Stack  Better Stack bundles uptime monitoring, incident management, on-call scheduling, log management, and status pages into one dashboard. For cloud monitoring, it sits closer to the external/uptime layer than to deep infra telemetry. It watches your cloud-hosted endpoints, collects logs, and gives you on-call and a status page without stitching together separate products.  The consideration is per-seat pricing. Every person who manages monitors or responds to incidents is a "responder" seat, so cost scales with team size rather than infrastructure size. Solo developers and small teams get a lot from the all-in-one bundle; larger on-call rotations should total the seat cost before committing.  Key strengths   All-in-one: uptime + logs + incident management + on-call + status pages  Clean, fast dashboard with a good free tier for getting started  Log management in the same platform as monitoring  Multi-cloud endpoint checks with global locations  Terraform provider for config-as-code   Pricing  Component Price Included Free $0/mo 10 monitors, 3-min intervals, 1 status page Responder $29/mo/seat (annual) Monitoring, incidents, on-call Additional monitors $21/50 monitors Added to any paid plan Logs Separate pricing Ingestion + retention-based  Cost traps   Per-seat pricing multiplies with team size. A 10-person rotation is $290/mo in seats alone  Monitor add-on packs stack up when you watch hundreds of endpoints  Log management is a separate meter from monitoring   Limitations   Not an infrastructure-metrics or APM platform. It's the external/uptime + logs layer  Response body validation is keyword-based, not JSON path  Deep container/Kubernetes telemetry isn't its focus   Best for: Small teams that want uptime monitoring, logs, on-call, and a status page in one place and are comfortable with per-seat pricing.  Decision framework  The right cloud monitoring tool depends on which half of the problem you're solving. Most teams eventually need both layers.  Start with your cloud shape. If you're all-in on one provider, the native tool (CloudWatch, Google Cloud Monitoring, or Azure Monitor) gives you the deepest, lowest-friction infrastructure telemetry with no new vendor. The moment you're genuinely multi-cloud, a native tool becomes one silo among several, and a cloud-agnostic platform (Datadog, New Relic, Dynatrace, Grafana Cloud) earns its cost.  Separate infra telemetry from external checks. Host metrics, traces, and logs answer "what is my infrastructure doing?" External checks and dependency correlation answer "is my service working for users, and is a vendor the reason it isn't?" Datadog, New Relic, and Dynatrace cover both at a price. If you already have infra metrics covered by a native tool, adding a focused external layer like DevHelm or Better Stack is often cheaper than upgrading to a full-stack suite.  Model total cost at your real scale. "Starting at $15/host" is not the bill. Usage-based tools grow with metric cardinality and log volume; per-seat tools grow with headcount; consumption tools grow with units you can't easily predict. Run the numbers for your host count, data volume, team size, and check frequency before signing anything.  Scenario Recommended Tool Why AWS-only, want native infra metrics Amazon CloudWatch Zero-setup AWS telemetry, no extra vendor GCP-only, want SLOs and traces Google Cloud Monitoring Native metrics, logs, and error-budget tracking Azure-only, want APM + logs Azure Monitor Application Insights + KQL log analytics Multi-cloud, want one full-stack pane Datadog or New Relic Infra + APM + logs across all clouds Enterprise, want AI root-cause Dynatrace OneAgent + Davis automation at scale Prometheus/Grafana shop Grafana Cloud Managed open-source stack, cloud-agnostic Have infra metrics, need external + dependency layer DevHelm Endpoint checks + vendor correlation at flat pricing Small team, want uptime + logs + on-call Better Stack All-in-one dashboard, per-seat pricing  Frequently asked questions  What is cloud monitoring?  Cloud monitoring is the practice of collecting metrics, logs, traces, and availability data from applications and infrastructure running in the cloud, then alerting when something degrades. In practice it splits into two layers: infrastructure monitoring (host, container, and service telemetry) and external monitoring (endpoint checks and third-party dependency correlation). Most teams end up running tools from both layers.  Which cloud monitoring software is best for AWS, Azure, or Google Cloud?  For single-provider shops, the native tool is usually the lowest-friction choice: CloudWatch for AWS, Azure Monitor for Azure, and Google Cloud Monitoring for GCP. They collect provider telemetry with no setup. The trade-off is lock-in. None of them is a strong multi-cloud pane of glass.  What are the best multi-cloud monitoring tools?  If you run workloads across two or more providers, a cloud-agnostic platform beats stitching native tools together. Datadog and New Relic are the most complete options for infra, APM, and logs across clouds. Grafana Cloud is the open-source-friendly choice. DevHelm covers the external layer (endpoint checks plus vendor-dependency correlation) without per-host pricing.  What should I use for Kubernetes and container monitoring?  For deep Kubernetes and container telemetry, Datadog, Dynatrace, New Relic, and Grafana Cloud (via Prometheus) all ingest pod, node, and cluster metrics. If you only need to know whether the services exposed by your cluster are reachable and correct from the outside, an external checker is a cheaper complement to cluster-level telemetry.  Is there open-source cloud monitoring software?  Yes. Prometheus with Grafana is the standard open-source stack, and Grafana Cloud is its managed form (Prometheus, Loki, Tempo). It's cloud-agnostic and covers metrics, logs, and traces, at the cost of more assembly and cardinality management than a turnkey tool.  How do I keep cloud monitoring costs under control?  Watch the meters that scale silently: metric cardinality, log ingestion and retention, per-host fees, and per-seat charges. Flat-rate tools (like DevHelm) and native pay-as-you-go services are the most predictable. Usage-based full-stack suites are the least. Model total cost at your real host count, data volume, and team size, not the advertised entry price.  What's the difference between cloud monitoring and observability?  Monitoring answers known questions ("is CPU high, is the endpoint up, did the error rate spike?") with metrics, dashboards, and alerts. Observability adds the ability to ask new questions after the fact by correlating high-cardinality metrics, traces, and logs. Full-stack platforms market themselves as observability; focused uptime and dependency tools market themselves as monitoring. Most teams need some of both.  What's the best cloud monitoring tool for startups?  Priorities for a startup or small SaaS team: a usable free tier, predictable pricing, and fast setup. New Relic's free tier and DevHelm's flat plans are both strong starting points. You get real coverage without an enterprise contract, and you can add infra-metrics depth later as you scale.  Related guides  If you want to go deeper on one slice of cloud monitoring, these guides pick up where this comparison leaves off.  Compare more monitoring tools   Best API monitoring tools — focused comparison of tools built for API health, latency, and response-contract validation.  Best website monitoring tools — how the leading uptime and page-monitoring tools compare on check types, probe regions, and alerting.  Best synthetic monitoring tools — scripted, multi-step checks that simulate real user journeys across your endpoints.  Best server monitoring tools — host agents, CPU/memory/disk metrics, and infra alert quality.  Best open-source monitoring tools — the Prometheus and Grafana ecosystem plus other self-hosted options.  Best monitoring tools for startups — lean, low-cost setups for small teams.  Best free monitoring tools — what you can actually monitor at $0, and where free tiers stop being enough.  Best incident management tools — how teams triage, track, and resolve incidents once an alert fires.  Datadog vs Dynatrace — head-to-head between the two enterprise full-stack platforms on features, AI analysis, and pricing.   Go deeper on the concepts   API uptime monitoring — external checks, response assertions, and multi-region confirmation for APIs.  Monitoring as code — defining monitors in version control with a CLI, Terraform, and SDKs.  Best status page software — options for a public or internal status page that reflects your monitor state.  Distributed tracing 101 — how tracing complements metrics and logs in an observability stack.  Monitoring and logging — how metrics-based monitoring and log analytics fit together.  What SSL errors mean and how to fix them — common certificate errors and how to catch expiries before users hit a warning.   The real question  Every tool on this list can draw a graph of your cloud. The ones that matter are the ones that answer the question you actually ask during an incident: what broke, and can I fix it, or is it someone else's cloud? Infrastructure-metrics platforms tell you your containers are healthy. They're less helpful when your app is degraded because a third-party API you depend on is having a bad day. That's a failure inside your service that isn't your infrastructure's fault.  If your infra telemetry is already handled by a native tool or a full-stack suite, the missing layer is usually external checks with response validation and dependency correlation. Knowing that checkout is down and that the common thread is Stripe. If you want that layer without a per-host or per-GB bill, try DevHelm's free tier : 50 monitors, response assertions, and resource-group correlation at $0, no credit card. If you need deep infrastructure metrics, APM, and log analytics across clouds, Datadog, New Relic, or a native tool will serve you better.  The worst outcome isn't picking the "wrong" tool. It's buying a full-stack observability platform to solve an uptime problem, or bolting an uptime checker onto a system that needed tracing. Match the tool to the half of the problem you actually have, and add the other half only when you feel its absence.
